paragraphs.text: ON THE FIRST BOOK OF KINGDOMS. There have been a great many prophets. We have not found their books, but we have learned their names from the history of Chronicles. Each of them wrote down what happened in his own time. So, for instance, among both the Hebrews and the Syrians the First Book of Kingdoms is called the Prophecy of Samuel. Those who composed the Books of Kingdoms drew their material from those writings, and they composed them a very long time afterward. For how could Samuel, who flourished with Saul, or even with David, have written what followed, down to the death of Nebuchadnezzar, who had taken Israel captive? And the things left out by those who compiled them [?].

And there was a man. He was one of the sons of Levi. Kohath was the father of Izhar, whose son was Korah, and whose descendant was Elkanah, the father of Samuel. The line of descent runs as follows: Kohath, Amminadab, Korah, Assir, Elkanah, Zuph, [?], Elihu, Jeroham, Elkanah.

The line of descent runs thus: Korah, Assir, Elkanah (1), Samuel. Eli was of the family of Ithamar. Because of his sons' drunken insolence, he and his whole line were stripped of the priestly honor. But how is Elkanah, who came from Armathaim, called an Ephrathite? Perhaps he happened to come from both cities: he had been born in Ephratha and brought up in Armathaim. In the same way the Savior, born in Bethlehem, was also called a Nazarene because of where he was brought up. C. L. And her voice was not heard. As Hannah prayed, only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. Then how did the writer come to record the words of the prayer? Only if one grants, as has been said (2), that those who bore the Spirit wrote down what happened in their time by the power of the Holy [Spirit] [?]. [?] that is, "I am a woman in hard straits": that is, afflicted, fasting. C. L. On the words "Do not give your handmaid over as (3) a daughter of pestilence (4)": Theodotion has "as one of the ignorant." Or else, just as it calls the wise man "understanding," so it calls the lawless son "of pestilence." C. L.

My heart is made firm. Hannah's hymn is admirable. She not only praises the Giver for what she has received, but also blends prophecy into her hymn and shares in her child's grace: having borne a prophet, she prophesies after the birth. Elizabeth too shared in John's grace, and Mary in that of Jesus. "I was shaken and fell into vain thoughts because I was childless. Now that my prayer has been granted, I am made firm in God, who has given me fine offspring." So it is clear that she had been made firm in faith when she asked for a child to be given her as a gift. C. L. My mouth is enlarged. "I too have gained the freedom to say, 'I am [no longer] barren' [?]." On the matter in which Peninnah and her people reproached me. For she turns to them and says what follows: "Do not boast, and do not speak." C. L. (1) Zuph, [?] Jeroham, Elkanah, Samuel; from the Augustan codex, in which what follows is not found. From Theodoret's [?]; see those on p. 282 [?].

[?] let Peninnah [not] pride herself [?] on human advantages. For by God's will both good fortune and bad fortune are subject to change. On "God prepares [his] designs": Symmachus has "and with him there are no pretexts." C. L. For the barren woman has borne seven. She proclaims beforehand the fruitfulness of the Church. For all time comes round in a cycle of seven days. And the Church's children filled the world, while the synagogue of the Jews, once rich in many children, prophets and righteous men, grew weak. For in the literal sense Hannah had borne only one child, Samuel. The bow of the mighty has grown weak. All these contrasts are a prophecy about the Church of the Gentiles and the Synagogue of the Jews: their positions are reversed, and grace passes over to the Gentiles (5). C. L. Those full of bread were diminished: Symmachus (6) and Theodotion have "those who were sated were diminished," instead of "they hired themselves out." C. L. And the hungry let go of the land. Aquila has "were crushed" [?]; Symmachus, "came to lack nothing." C. L. The Lord puts to death [?] and makes alive. She foretells not only the general resurrection, but also that Christ (7) was going to raise the souls of many saints together with himself, just as he also raised their bodies for a time. This was so that it might be known that their souls had been freed from their age-long bonds and had passed to other places, to heaven and paradise. C. L. The Lord makes poor and makes rich. Again she foretells what is to come. For Saul, once exalted, is brought low, while David is raised up from the sheepfolds (8). What follows also belongs to this sense and this prediction. To seat him with princes. The disciples will have twelve thrones, and the rest of the faithful will be at rest, which is what the throne signifies. C. L. Granting the prayer to the one who prays: that is, bringing to completion those people who please God. C. L. The Lord will make weak [his adversary]. She foretells the overthrow of the devil. "[Let not] the wise man [boast in his wisdom], but let [the one who boasts] boast in this." It did not say, "Let one boast in this, in acting justly." First it laid faith as a foundation on the rock, which is Christ, and only then did it enjoin virtue. C. L. The Lord went up into the heavens and thundered. She prophesies the Savior's ascension, the coming of the all-holy Spirit, and the loud voice of the apostolic
[?] daughter [?] being animate, and he made the bodies for a time [?]

proclamation, and the second coming of Christ. "For he himself," it says, "will judge the ends of the earth, since he is righteous." She also foretells his ancestors according to the flesh, who lasted from David until the captivity: "For he will give strength," it says, "to our kings." And she did much to humble the pride of the arrogant, declaring beforehand to men that all knowledge and every pursuit is divine and comes from God [?]

Girded with an ephod bar and a small double cloak. Aquila has "a choice outer garment"; Symmachus, "a linen ephod and a small mantle"; Theodotion, "an ephod bar and a small outer robe." But how could Samuel, a Levite, use the ephod, when it was reserved for the high priest alone? Probably Eli saw divine grace blossoming in him. The boy had been born in a wonderful way, promised before his mother's labor, and brought up inside the divine tabernacle. So Eli granted him this honor, very young though he was, as one who was holy and a Nazirite, as his name also shows. Through the ephod God revealed beforehand a great many things that were unknown. I said, "Your house and your father's house." The prediction seems to strip Eli's family of the high priesthood, but it hints at the end of the whole Jewish [priesthood]. For he says, "I said, 'Your house and your father's house will walk before me forever.'" He made this promise not to Ithamar but to Aaron. So he pronounced sentence against their whole tribe, and what we see bears witness to it. And you will look upon the strength of temples. The saying is obscure [?]. Symmachus rendered it thus: "And you will see a rival [?] of the dwelling in all with which Israel will be blessed." Others read it as "the strength of the One who Is" and interpreted it thus: it speaks of the God who is. For "I am," he says, "the One who Is." The strength of this One possesses the priesthood after the order of Melchizedek. Eli paid the penalty for his sons, even though he had given them fitting advice. For they needed something stronger than gentle remedies. After a first and a second warning they should have been driven out of the sacred precincts, since they were teaching others to break the law as well. And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest. These words fit no human being, but only our Lord Jesus Christ, who has been named our high priest, since he offers the sacrifice on our behalf to the Father. And by "anointed ones" he means the holy apostles and those who took up their teaching after them. Properly, then, the prediction applies to Christ, but in terms of the history it applies to Zadok, who traced his line from Eleazar and received the high priesthood through Solomon.
And the lamp of God, before it was trimmed. It shows that it was right after evening, when they had begun

to sleep, that God appeared to Samuel. For they used to light the sacred lamp in the evening and add oil around midnight. So the writer, wishing to indicate the time, said that the lamp had not yet been tended. God honored such youth above grey hair. He passed over the man who had lived ninety-eight years and had held a double office for forty years, for Eli was both judge and high priest. Instead he spoke with a very small child, teaching how much better youth adorned with virtue is than grey hair. God turned away from Eli only because of his sons, for Eli was plainly adorned with good deeds of his own. First, he was not ashamed to urge the youth to tell him what God had announced, and he bound him with an oath and with curses to hide nothing. Then, when he learned the verdict, he uttered a praiseworthy word: "The Lord will do what is pleasing in his sight." Nor did he bear his sons' slaughter ignobly, father and old man though he was. It was because of the captured ark that he fell, and in his deep despair he died. It shall not be atoned. Here he seems in some way to block repentance, giving them no hope of pardon. But pay attention to the saying. He says, "With sacrifices I do not pardon them"; that is, unless it is through works and complete repentance. "For the sin is not a simple one, that they might appease me with livestock; the insult has reached up to me." C. L.

And the ark of God was taken. What happened produced a double benefit. It taught the Hebrews that when they live according to the law they should take courage in God's providence, but when they break the law they should trust neither in him nor in the ark. For why, while breaking the law, did they take the ark into war as a help, when it held the law stored up inside it? The Philistines, for their part, were benefited when they were afraid, when the Hebrews raised a shout as the ark appeared. But after their victory they grew contemptuous and dedicated the ark to their own idols as a kind of first-fruits of the spoils, and so they learned God's might by experience. And he judged Israel twenty years. The Hebrew has forty, for it reads "arbaim." All the others also rendered it this way.

And he struck them in their hindparts. Aquila says they suffered from a gangrenous ulcer. Josephus says dysentery, which does not disagree with Scripture, since a belly that runs uncontrollably also tends to afflict the anus. They suffered this affliction of the seat because they had impiously seated the divine ark beside a falsely named god. [?] (2) L. "Arbaeim."

The [?] say. They suspected that the blow was not sent by God but was a disease caused by some pestilential condition, so they moved the ark to themselves and suffered the same things. And the ark of God was in the field of the Philistines seven months. Since no city dared to receive the ark, they left it outside in the open, thinking that this would rid them of the blow. Because of this they were also punished in the fruits of the earth, God persuading them [?], just as he had also brought the various plagues on the Egyptians. For the memory of those plagues was still ringing in their ears, as their own words testify. In a box, beergaz [?]: Symmachus has "Put it in the little chest at its side"; Aquila, [?]; and Josephus calls the box "argoze" [?]. God condescended and went along with the opinion of the diviners. For the achievement is all the greater when the enemies themselves bear witness to God's power and their own teachers pronounce the verdict on it. From a fortified city, and what follows. Aquila says "strong"; Symmachus, "walled." As far as an unwalled village, and as far as the great Abel, by which they set down the ark of the Lord. Who will be able to stand by? That is, "to stand" and "to withstand" before the Lord, as the others render it. The sons of Jeconiah, being impious and serving idols, were displeased when they saw the ark, and they paid the penalty. The people, for their part, were disciplined because they had not been willing to risk danger for the ark. They had left it with the Philistines for seven months and had not taken up war on its behalf.

And the groves of Ashtaroth. Aquila puts it thus: "the statues of Astarte." That is what they call Aphrodite, naming her after the star, for their myth says that the morning star is hers. And Samuel took a suckling lamb. Before the divine temple was built, they worshiped God in various places. Knowing how ready the people were to fall into impiety, he confined divine worship to one place. But for the pious, who understood the purpose of the law, every place was consecrated to the worship of God. Indeed the great Elijah built an altar on Carmel and offered sacrifice there, even though God's temple, according to the law, summoned everyone to itself.
And his sons did not walk in his way. Then how is it that Samuel did not pay the penalty for his sons C. L. adds here: "and some [?] like a wild olive; others

as Eli did? Their offenses were wrongs, not impieties like those of Eli's sons, who defiled the divine tabernacle with their lusts and snatched the first portions of the sacrifices. These sons are accused of taking bribes, and Samuel knew nothing of it. For he lived far from his sons, in Armathaim, while they lived in Beersheba. And the thing was evil in Samuel's sight. Because the request was contrary to the divine law. For God himself filled the role of king for them, and the prophet served under him, like a general or a leader of the people.

A man of fine stature, and good. He is not testifying to any virtue of soul in him, but to his looks and his size; for it explains that it calls him good in body. Look, I have a quarter of a shekel in my hand. This was Saul's supposition, not bribe-taking on the prophet's part. Saul guessed that something ought to be offered to Samuel as a ruler and a prophet. But he offered nothing; on the contrary, he was treated with kindness. If prophets had customarily taken payment, Micah the prophet would not have said, "And her prophets prophesied for silver." Understand in the same way what Jeroboam said to his wife in the Third Book of Kingdoms, when his child fell ill and he sent her to Ahijah the Shilonite to ask him about the child. There too Jeroboam is seen telling his wife to take gifts to the prophet, yet in Scripture the prophet is nowhere seen taking them. So it was wicked men who might falsely suspect such things of prophets, who either took nothing or took only from the righteous. For taking something is not blameworthy in itself, since the apostles too did so [?] when others ministered to them. As Paul also says, "Even twice you sent me help for my need." Look, a testimony; set it before you. He set this before him as one who was about to reign and to face danger on the people's behalf. That is why he calls it a testimony. For "testimony" Symmachus rendered "what was left over," and for "what has been set aside for you as a testimony," he rendered "what has been kept for you on purpose." For "from the people," Theodotion rendered "for it was said, 'I have invited the people'"; Aquila, "saying, 'the people' [?]".
And he kissed him. So as to share with him the grace that dwelt in himself. He gives him many signs, because he saw that he was doubtful and

was confessing his own poverty. This is why he confirms the promise of the kingdom with predictions. And you will be changed into another man. Since Saul was a rustic who knew only how to farm, God appointed him king and gave him a kingly mind. Is Saul also among the prophets? Symmachus has "Is Saul still too [?]" He did not have the gift of prophecy permanently, but he prophesied at that time as a sign of the spiritual gift. So too the seventy elders were granted the gift of prophecy as soon as Moses chose them, but not afterward; instead, being made wise by God, they settled the people's disputes. His kinsman. Aquila says "his father's

brother." And the tribe of Benjamin is taken by lot. Those who lived in wickedness did not believe even the divine prophets. So that they would not suspect that the choice came from human favor, he left the decision to the lot, through which God showed what he had decided. When Saul was chosen by lot, he tried to hide, seeing that the authority was beyond his worth. But when God pointed him out to the prophet, he received his appointment over all the people.

By gouging out the right eye of every one of you. He wanted to make them useless for war. For the left eye is covered by the shield, while the right eye watches the enemy, and whoever loses it is easily captured. In the same way the evil powers hasten to cut away the right side of our thoughts.

Testify against me before the Lord. As judge, he was stepping down from his authority and handing it over to the king. By speaking about his own conduct and gaining the people's agreement, he taught them the king's lawful authority. And now stand still, and I will judge you before the Lord, and what follows. Symmachus has: "And now present yourselves, so that I may plead with you before the Lord concerning all the mercies of the Lord that he has done."

Saul was a year old when he began to reign. Symmachus rendered it: "Saul was like a child of one year." This shows the simplicity of soul that Saul had when he began to reign, which he did not keep for very long. Hence it adds: And he reigned two years over Israel, that is, with simplicity. After that he turned aside to wickedness and was stripped of divine grace. So the rest of the time he reigned is reckoned to Samuel's leadership. And Jonathan struck Nasib. Aquila

rendered it "the garrison." The others [?] "for the appointment" [?]; [?] "for the appointed time" [?]; Theodotion, "for the time." For Samuel had instructed Saul to wait seven days for him and only then, after offering an acceptable sacrifice, to draw up for battle. But when Saul saw the Philistines gathered, he did not wait for the prophet as he had been commanded, and for this reason the loss of his kingdom is foretold to him. And I have not entreated the face of the Lord. But [?] tool [?], small axe, mattock [?] [Latin:] [?] ploughshare [?], and his [?]; adze, [?] his [?]. Aquila
my [?] (symbolically), [?] the will [?] of God. Each man's sword was against his neighbor. For they killed one another without recognizing each other, since they were mixed together

[?] Saul pronounced a curse foolishly; why then did God [?] confirm the curse? First he convicts Saul of having cursed foolishly; then he teaches that not even such curses are to be despised. In this case Saul's aim was pious, for he was looking [?] to God's honor. But he ought to have considered that the toil of fighting inevitably brings thirst as well. Jonathan acted in ignorance, and though he had this in his defense, he was nevertheless in danger of his very life. But he was set free because the people justly pleaded his cause.

I regret that I anointed Saul as king. God's regret is a change in his dispensation. God put Saul forward because of his attractive body. He did not himself value this, for he is the maker of all things; he did it because of the people, who admire only what is beautiful to the senses. For Zacchaeus, though small, received the Master. Samuel, though young, was granted the divine appearance. And David was preferred to his bigger, older brothers. For God does not value size or grey hair above virtue. So he says "I regret" in human fashion, since he is speaking to human beings, and rustic ones at that, and is indicating that the kingdom will pass to David. Let me be, and I will tell you. Though he is a prophet, he asks for leave to speak freely, since he is speaking to a king. He reminds him of what he had said before he became king. Because I listened to the voice of the people. Saul uses Adam's words to the prophet. It is like "The woman you gave to be with me, she gave it to me." Look, the Lord does not want whole burnt offerings. This is because Saul had said that he had brought the herds and flocks to offer as sacrifice. For rebellion is the sin of divination. Iniquity and teraphim bring pain and toil. Symmachus has: "For contentiousness is the sin of divination, and disobedience is the iniquity of idols." So he treated disobedience to God as equal to impiety. Someone says that perhaps it hints at the folly of certain people who suspected that it was a bad omen for victors not to profit from the spoil. Just as the ephod was dedicated to God, and through it those who inquired were shown what they should do, so the predictions of the idols were revealed through the teraphim. God foresaw Saul's later transgressions as well, but the present one alone was enough to bring the ultimate punishment on him. For he ought to have understood that God's love for humanity surpasses all human goodness. Yet Saul thought he would appear more humane than God [?] [?] C. N. to disobey [?].

[?] ... of the spoil, he came back bringing the best of it. Yet when he himself had decreed that no one should take food, he hurried to enforce his own decree and showed no pity, not even sparing his son. God had devoted Amalek to destruction, not because of their impiety toward him but because of their cruelty toward his people. Yet Saul [?] took the best of the spoil and was not taught restraint even by the example of Achan. If God had overlooked Amalek's punishment until then, this too came from his love for humankind. He had given them so much room for repentance and waited for their sins to reach their full measure, but instead of repenting they kept adding to them. And yet so many wonders had been done for Israel, which ought to have made them turn back. If it was their ancestors who sinned and these are the ones punished, it is first because the measure was filled up in their time, since they added so much. Second, because there is a judgment, those earlier ones did not escape punishment either. And by being punished these became an example to the rest, since both the punishments of this life and those of the life to come are measured by what is deserved. The timing may differ because of God's dispensation, and even these did not pay their full due here. For how could one punishment in the present be enough for many great impieties? Otherwise nothing would be more blessed than sinners who are punished here. A nation is judged as a nation, and individuals each according to what they deserve. "And Samuel slew Agag." As Phinehas slew Zimri. For whatever God commands is pious. CHAPTER 16. "How shall I go? Saul will hear of it," and so on. As a man, he is afraid and offers this objection. He was told to go on the pretext of a sacrifice, but this was no lie, for God does not teach lying, and he really did offer the sacrifice. He was told, then, to keep the deed hidden but to speak of the

Why does he not name David, but say "one of the sons of Jesse"? So that David would not suffer from his brothers what Joseph suffered from his. So ignorance is the mother of safety. Or the prophet did not know who was being sought, because God was keeping him within modest limits. For knowledge of all things belongs to God alone. C. L. "And he saw Eliab," and so on. If Samuel had gone straight to David, he would have seemed to act out of some prejudice. By going through all of them, he showed that God had rejected the others and chosen David. Even after this had happened, the brothers laid bare their envy when they saw David at the battle line. What would they not have done if it had not happened?

having the deadness that comes from sin, and [?] ... Jacob. But David was ruddy and had beautiful eyes, which show David's keen perception [?] and the vigour of his soul. This is not praise of the body. God chose him after he had been trained beforehand in shepherding, and had learned to rule people by caring for the ewes as they gave birth. C. L. "And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit seized him." When the divine Spirit departed, the evil spirit found room. In the same way, when apostolic grace left Judas, the devil entered into him. As usual, Scripture attributes the cause of the evil spirit's indwelling to God. This is not because God gave it, but because when he took away the holy Spirit, the evil one gained an opening to do as it pleased. The divine Spirit had been given to Saul when he was anointed king, so it was fitting that when he fell from the kingship the Spirit should depart with it to the man appointed in his place, and that its opposite should find room. Otherwise, evil spirits are given no authority over anyone without divine permission. C. L. "A man who knows how to play." God did not give worship with musical instruments, but David devised it with great piety. He burned with longing for God, and so he turned to piety the things that inflame people to licentiousness, blending melody and articulate voice with divine hymns. In this way the melody would stir the senses and the meaning would kindle longing for God along with it. David, then, had received the working of the divine Spirit, and while the Spirit was at work the evil spirit kept quiet. "And the man is prudent, and a warrior." How could one who tended sheep be called a man, prudent in speech, and a warrior? The speaker, then, was not speaking on his own, but foretold the future as if it were present and bore witness to what David was going to be. C. L. CHAPTER 17. "Saul gave him his armour, and David could not carry it." God did not allow it, so that David would win without armour and the armour would not claim the credit for the victory. C. L. "And all the earth will know that there is a God in Israel." As he draws up for battle, he prophesies and foretells that the whole world will come to know God. "And he struck the foreigner." He kills the foreigner with a stone, foreshadowing the stone cut without hands, who is descended from him according to the flesh. C. L. And he used the foreigner's own sword to kill him, to foreshadow the Saviour's victory [?]. [?] Up to this point these things [are found] in ... [?]. ... in the ... of the Augustan [codex] [?] ... according to the ... [?].

[vic]tory. For the one who nailed the Master to the cross was thrown down from his tyranny through the cross. This fulfilled the saying, "The sinner is caught in the works of his own hands." C. L. "Whose son is this young man?" How did Saul not know David? Either because in his madness he had not noticed David when he played the lyre, or because envy drove him to find out exactly where he came from. "Loving him as his own soul." Aquila: "according to his own soul." The divine law also commands this: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself."

"And his mandyas." A kind of outer cloak. "I think," he says, "it is an Arcadian garment, or what most people call a mantion." The Seventy say "torn garments" of the man who brought news that Eli's sons had been killed, but Aquila rendered it [?] "mandyas." And the king of the Ammonites cut off half of the cloaks of David's envoys, up to the fold at their hips. "And an evil spirit fell upon Saul, and he prophesied," and so on. The word is used loosely. Scripture calls false prophets prophets, and falsely named gods gods. False prophets were like madmen, as Saul was. He had been stripped of divine grace, while David, by playing, calmed the demon's frenzy and stilled Saul's envy. It was not that Saul prophesied because he had received the Holy Spirit. How could he share at the same time in an evil spirit and the Holy Spirit? Rather, the evil spirit was choking him and made him say such things: that he would be deprived of the kingdom, and that it would pass to the very man his envy was aimed at. The same happened with Paul and Silas, when the woman who had the spirit of Python cried out, "These men are servants of the Most High God." For when God wills it, even demons are forced to confess the truth. "And the Lord Almighty was with him." This is how he named the all-holy Spirit, for David had been found worthy of this grace. "Let my hand not be upon him, but let the hand of the foreigners be upon him." The story showed Saul's purpose: the marriage was a plot, not a kindness. "But only a hundred foreskins of foreigners." Why not heads? Because Saul suspected that David would kill some of his own countrymen and bring their heads. That is why he asks for foreskins, which prove that the dead were foreigners.

Still, Saul was a slave to envy and kept watching for a chance to kill David. When David was saved by Michal, he sang the fifty-eighth psalm: "Deliver me from my enemies, O God." C. L. This is like the saying, "If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two." David was ordered to kill a hundred foreigners, and he killed two hundred, trampling on Saul's malice, as the text renders it. C. L.

"And Michal took the cenotaphs," and so on. Aquila says "figures," and "the goats' liver" is [?] the whole mass, a ball of hair. After helping David escape, she made the bed look like a sick man lay in it, heaping clothes on it and putting a ball of hair under the clothes to look like a head. Some say the "figures" were an image of David, which she covered with the clothes except for some parts of the face. She used the goats' liver because some say it keeps moving for a long time after the animal is slaughtered. "And the Spirit of God came upon Saul's messengers, and they prophesied." How did these men prophesy? And how did Saul prophesy later? The Master's snares are of many kinds. Some people he catches through other people, and others he catches with blindness, as happened in Elisha's time. These he prevented from killing David by prophetic grace. Saul came after all of them, and he too was caught in the bonds of God's love for humankind. He did prophesy, but not as the others did. Because he was unworthy of the grace, he lay stripped of his clothes all day long, and this posture signified that the kingdom was being taken from him. He was also paying the penalty for despising the prophetic Spirit, since by his anger against David he had insulted the divine Spirit. From this it is clear that whoever clings to the saints will be holy, even if he was wicked before, especially if he does not run back to his former ways.

"[Unless] he reveals it to my ear." Symmachus: "Unless he makes it known to my hearing." C. L. For "It is filled between me" and what follows, Aquila and Symmachus have: "There is only a step between me and death." C. L. "He loved the soul of the one who loved him." Aquila: "as his own soul." C. L. For "Your seat will be missed," Symmachus has "will be sought." C. L. "You will do it on the third day." Aquila: "You will wait three days." Why did Jonathan use arrows, that is, darts, to tell David about his father's plot? Some say it was because of the servant, so that he would not learn the message. But Jonathan could have come alone. Yet he would not have [escaped] the sus- [?] "Symmachus" is not found in the Augustan codex.

-picion, if he had gone alone, of telling David about the plot. So he goes out with the boy and pretends to be practising archery. Through his words to the servant he hints to David that he should flee, and after sending the servant ahead he advises David to flee. "On the day of the work." Aquila: "of the deed." He calls the first flight "the work." For "Ergab" the other translators rendered "stone." "To the lamattara." Aquila: "to the target," or "to the guard-post," for the text is read two ways. Symmachus: "to the appointed place." The interpretation of Hebrew words gives it thus: among the Greeks a ditch, among the Romans a fossa, among the Syrians a target, at which they practise shooting arrows. Some say it was a hollow place where David sat and from which he rose. "As once and once" means "as was his custom." "Some mishap has befallen him." Saul thought David had excused himself from the feast because he was unclean and not purified, and so he said nothing. "Because he was broken over David." Aquila: [?]; Symmachus: "was pained"; Theodotion: "was grieved." That is, Jonathan was moved and pitied David, who was being plotted against by his father. "To finish him," that is, to kill him outright. C. L. "To the appointment of David" means that he brought him where he had promised David he would come. Theodotion: "passed over." C. L. "And David rose from Annegab." Aquila: "next to the back." Perhaps there was a hollow place there. [The other translators rendered "stone." C. Lip.]

"To Ahimelech." In the title of the thirty-third psalm, the book of Psalms has Abimelech instead of Ahimelech. One letter was exchanged for another because the letter the Hebrews call [?] looks like Kaph. The two letters are alike and differ only by a very tiny stroke. And how is it that the Saviour, when he mentions this story in the Gospels, says "in the time of Abiathar the high priest"? Either Ahimelech had two names and was also called Abiathar, or one must say that while Ahimelech [?] ... Abiathar happened to be high priest at that time. The book of Kings evidently says that Ahimelech and the priests of God were killed by Saul, but it does not say a high priest was. It should be noted that the learned among the former people cared less about the bodily precepts of the law. That is why David did what the law of Moses did not allow, eating the loaves of presentation. And the priest too, by giving them to him, and [Footnotes:] "Symmachus: was pained" is not in the Augustan codex. "Passed over" [?] ... Aquila: "arrows." The same. [?] ... brought the [?]. The same.

he thought more deeply than most people. In asking whether the young men were clean from women, he showed that purity and chastity give people honour equal to that of priests. Read this as a question, that is: "And would anyone call this way profane, when it has been sanctified because of my vessels," that is, my armour, and because I am going out to war? It is clear from this that the young men were armour-bearers who carried his weapons and kept themselves pure whenever he went out to war. Many passages show that the young men followed him as armour-bearers. One is near the end of First Kingdoms, where it says, "And Saul said to the man who carried his armour, 'Draw your sword and run me through with it.'" Another is near the end of the Second, in the list of David's mighty men: "Gelore the Beerothite, armour-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah." So this is what David means here: the young men are purified because they are armour-bearers, even though at that moment, since he was fleeing, he was carrying no weapons. C. L. When David shared in what had been assigned to the priests, he foreshadowed the mystical table set before all the faithful. For priests and people alike, all who have shared in divine baptism, partake of the Master's body. The Saviour also showed that David was not to be blamed for eating, since he told this story to defend his disciples. C. L. "And this way is profane." Having said that they had kept themselves pure for three days, he added that because of the task before him he must of necessity share in the sacred food, so that it would strengthen him to accomplish what lay ahead. He used "profane" to mean not "unclean" but "not sacred," which is why Aquila rendered it [?]. That is: even if I am not a priest, I have received prophetic grace. Their vessels and full armour are the spiritual gift. "For there is no other here besides it." It was not permitted to store weapons of war in God's tabernacle. But this sword had been dedicated there as a thank-offering, in memory of the victory, to the one who had given the victory. "And he feigned on that day, and drummed." Aquila: "he went limp and kept striking."

Saul's slaughter of the priests was more impious than his other crimes. For when God had commanded him to wipe out Amalek completely, he disobeyed, and [?] ... [Footnote:] The passage from "that" to "David" is not contained in the [?] codex. ... all of us who believe partake.

"And his business was in Carmel." Eusebius says that here it does not mean the mountain, but a village still called by that name today, in which Nabal lived. "And five ephahs of barley meal." Aquila translated "seahs." The gomor is equal to the ephah, as in Ezekiel [?]

"Perhaps I guarded all Nabal's goods for an unjust man." Aquila: "surely in vain." How could a man who showed such meekness toward Saul try to kill Nabal? David had done Nabal a great deal of good. He had not only restrained his own men but also kept others from plotting against him, as Nabal's servants testified when they said, "The men were very good to us." Even so, when David asked out of need, Nabal would not give him even a modest amount, and he insulted him besides. Saul at least had a reason for his hostility, namely his envy over the kingdom. But no less [?] ...

[COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF ... [?]] ... is contrary to "If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil." Yet he hurries to kill not only Nabal but all his household. To this one must reply that he did not repay evil, because he was prevented by the providence of God, which makes up for what the saints lack. Perhaps that is why he says, "I said in my prosperity, 'I shall never be moved.' Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty, but you turned your face away, and I was troubled." Such abandonments happen so that the saints will not become proud, as with Peter at his denial and with Paul and the angel of Satan. That is also why David loved so dearly the woman who served as providence's instrument, as was natural, since she had stood in the way of his passion. "Nabal" means "folly," as the woman says and as the interpretation of Hebrew names has handed down. [?] Aquila rendered: "[?] is with him." For when reason drains away and is extinguished, the passion of folly arises. These things could also be applied to the first people, who were ungrateful and repaid Christ with evil for good. Since then the worship of God has passed over to the new David, through whom they did not perish completely but received pardon for their folly when Christ said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." Among them he looked for food and found none, just as with the fig tree, which is a type of the synagogue of the Jews. Why then did David break his oath, when he had sworn to kill Nabal and those with him? One must reply that the oath came from just anger, while the sparing came from sober reason. When he accepted Abigail's plea, he put out his anger. It is better to go beyond the limit of a threat than to commit such slaughter. "One who urinates against a wall." No one stands and urinates against a wall unless he has nothing else to do. So he means even someone who is carefree and expects no harm. Or "one who urinates against a wall" means someone weak, who cannot stand without leaning on the wall. Others have said it means a dog, since this is a dog's habit. It is as if he said, "I will not leave so much as a dog." "On me, my lord, be the iniquity" means, she says, "count it against me, as though I were the one who did wrong." She says this though she did no wrong, so that the righteous David might forgive her the wrongdoer's deeds. C. L. [?] Abigail altered the name Nabal into [?] an interjection of lament. For such a man also deserved to be lamented. C. L. "And the souls of your enemies you will sling away," he says. He means this: even if you are ever caught in the middle of your enemies as if in a sling, you will not be shaken out or slung away, but your enemies will be shaken out. "And this will not be an abomination to you." Aquila: [?]

and he hints at the stings of conscience. ["In the lampene," a covered carriage. Aquila says "in the circle." [?] ... the shape of the arrangement, which shows that the king was surrounded by the camp.] "Unless the Lord strikes him." As he struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, the people many times in the wilderness, and Nabal the Carmelite. "Or his day comes" refers to natural death [?]

[He does not], however, say that the day is fixed. It is fixed for everyone in general that they must die, but for each person it is not yet [known] when it will be. C. L. "For a stupor from the Lord had fallen on them." For "amazement" Aquila has "deep sleep"; Symmachus, "torpor"; Theodotion, "trance." C. L. "You are sons of death, you who guard your lord the king, the Lord's anointed." "You are sons of death" means "you deserve to die." David took the spear and the jar of water back, to show the kindness he had done. C. L. [They said,] "Go, serve other gods." They did not say this in words, but they forced him to do it by their actions. By driving him out from everywhere, they compelled him to take refuge in the foreigners' cities as strongholds. David had great and wonderful virtue: though he suffered so much, he did not take revenge when he could, because of his surpassing meekness. That is why he says boldly in the Psalms, "Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness." C. L. CHAPTER [?]. "So be it: I will make you chief of my bodyguard all your days." "Chief of my bodyguard" means "guardian of my head." C. L. "And Samuel died." Because he was about to tell the story of the medium, he had to mention Samuel's death again. "And Saul disguised himself." Instead of "disguised himself," Symmachus said "changed his appearance." This signified the transfer of the kingdom. C. L. "A man coming up, standing upright." Some say she truly brought up Samuel. What could be more impious than this, if people practising occult arts could gain power over the souls of the saints, over whom the demons had no power while they were still alive? Either, then, a demon fabricated Samuel's appearance and played his part, saying things it had often heard from Samuel, though it did not know when Saul would die [?] ... [Footnote:] "This" is not found in [?] the Augustan codex [?] ...

[?]…a divine angel shaped the appearance as he wished, since God delivers his sentence even through what is contrary, as he says: "And if he goes to the false prophet, I the Lord will answer him." In this way he blessed the people through Balaam and proclaimed in advance the salvation of the world, through the working of the divine Spirit. Now too he caused the form of Samuel to appear [?]. In the same way Scripture called the angels who appeared to Abraham, and their Master, "men", because that is how the patriarch seemed to see them. That is why he also set a table before them. In the same way Scripture calls "gods" those who are not gods. So now it says "Samuel", so that Saul would believe this, receive his rejection from it, and leave this life groaning. If we think it was Samuel because the name is used, then it is also time to regard as truly gods the "gods" she says she saw, although there is only one who is God by nature. Some say that Samuel really did appear, but that God presented his soul and the medium did not bring it up. Divine Scripture says only that she saw Samuel, not that she herself brought him up. In acts of necromancy, people used to see shadowy phantoms through the deceptions of demons. One might say that the speaker's ignorance about Saul's death shows that it was a demon. Saul evidently died not "tomorrow" but some days later. Perhaps "tomorrow" only shows that his death was near. Or else Scripture narrated the events concerning David and Amalek ahead of time, before Saul's death. That is what those who say Samuel truly appeared would argue. Or at any rate it was some similar form produced by divine power.

"And the satraps of the Philistines were passing by." This is a recapitulation. "He has fallen over to me": Symmachus has "he has fled to me." "They were grieved": Aquila has "they were provoked", Symmachus "they were angered", and Theodotion "they were enraged." "And David said to Achish, What have I done to you, and what have you found in your servant?" He kept up the appearance of goodwill toward the Philistines, even to the point of marching against Israel. He did not mean to fight, but perhaps to join in attacking the Philistines, which is just what they suspected. Or else he expected God to prevent it, which is what happened. "He shall not go with us into battle." This too was the work of divine providence. Otherwise he would either have turned against the people of Israel and filled himself with kindred blood, or he would not have stood by while the people perished. But God made every provision both for the people and for Saul, whom it was necessary [?]…

…[?] God [pre]served the wives of David's men. [?] "Bring the ephod": Aquila has "bring near to me." Among the Hebrews the words are "the band" and "the raiding party". This is the name for a gang of robbers. Aquila rendered it "of a lightly armed band." [?]

"And the seventy men stayed behind": Aquila has "were too exhausted to cross over." "Because I was sick": Aquila has "I fell ill." "From the morning star": Aquila has "from the dark of the moon" and Symmachus "from when it grew dark." This stands for "I fell ill on the third day", that is, for three days.

ON THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGDOMS. "He fell by a fall" means that Israel was defeated. For "they overtook him", Aquila has [?]… "The armlet" is a gold ornament worn either on the upper arm or on the wrist. Aquila called it a "bracelet". "For your mouth has answered against you." What a philosophical soul! When he heard of the slaughter of his enemy, he lamented bitterly. The messenger, who had suffered no wrong, mocked the dead man. He did this even though Jonathan had fallen with Saul, together with a very large army. He also falsely claimed to be the slayer. He was an Amalekite, too, and God had long before pronounced a sentence of death against that people. So some people are wrong to blame David over this. "And David lamented." Many things produced the lament: his longing for Jonathan, his affection for the people, the victory of the impious Philistines, and, besides these, the slaughter of Saul. He had revered Saul while he lived, and he pitied him far more once he was dead. "It is written," it says, "in the Book of the Upright." This shows that [?] from many prophetic [?]…

…the history was written. We must ask whether lamenting befits a philosopher, and for whom one should lament. We must also ask whether he lamented for those who died or for himself, as did those who mourned over Stephen. "Set up a pillar, Israel": Aquila has "be exact." He says this was no ordinary blow. The one who fell was a king and a king's son, along with the best of his countrymen. What follows shows that the power of the Philistines grieved him greatly. "Set up a pillar, Israel" means: keep this fall before you like a pillar standing on a height. In other words, remember the present blow and seek its cause…

"Fields of firstfruits": Aquila has "of offerings" and Theodotion "of death." "The shield was rejected": Aquila has "was cast away." "Mountains of Gilboa." In his pain he curses lifeless things. People suffering in some part of the body do the same: they cannot bear the pain and pound their hands against the walls or the bed. The passage may also point to something higher: Christ lamenting the first people, the finer souls among them, and the way the worship of the Law stood above the Gentiles. For he said, "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets," and so on. Their death is being deprived of the gifts from heaven, as in the words "Behold, your house is left to you desolate."

"Your love was like the love of women." He says this to show how warm and genuine his affection was. A husband's disposition toward his wife is such that the law about marriage says: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." Elkanah showed this too when he comforted Hannah: "Am I not better to you than ten children?" What is "one flesh" for those who marry is "one soul" for those who love. "Shall the sword devour for ever?" He says it is not just for victors to try to bring total destruction on the defeated. Victors are often defeated, and pursuers often flee. That is why he says that the end will be bitter. He also reminded him of their kinship, and persuaded him. The words "the end will be bitter" mean that making war on one's brothers [brings] regret…
"And he said, To Hebron." Judging from what appears, one can say it was because the patriarchs had lived and were buried there. It was also because of the tribe of Judah, from which…
…David came, Hebron was then the chief city. For still [?]…

"And the fourth, [?]": Aquila has "Adonijah." "Why did you go in to my father's concubine?" Those who were not kings were not allowed to lie with the concubines of kings. That is why Absalom had relations with his father's concubines, wanting to secure the kingdom. Adonijah too was put to death for his tyrannical designs, because he wanted to marry his father's concubine. "Unless you bring up Michal." Yet it is unlawful to take back a woman who has been joined to another man. God says through Jeremiah: "If a man sends away his wife, and she goes and becomes another man's, will she ever return to him again?" But David had not divorced [his wife]. Saul had torn her away unlawfully and betrothed her to another man. That is why David excused the force used. "From the expedition": Aquila has "from the gedud, a lightly armed band." "And he struck him there." Joab's stated reason, the killing of Asahel, was real, but the actual cause was envy. He knew that Abner would be given the command if he brought all Israel over to the king. So out of love of power he committed murder. "And holding a staff." By the law, a man with a discharge and a leper are unclean and are excluded from the common life. Those maimed in body use a staff. That is why Aquila [renders] such a person as "blind"…

…[?] The one was harsh, unjust and ungracious. Abner was fair in his dealings [?], and because he was brave in battle he did not suffer the fate of the defeated. It was pretended friendship that brought slaughter upon him. David lamented in his grief, and the lament increased the people's goodwill. "The sons of Zeruiah are harder than I." He gives the reason why he did not kill Joab on account of Abner. Where it is easy to use just anger, he shows no restraint.

"And they anoint David" [?]. This means that the other tribes elect him. "Because the lame and the blind resisted." The Jebusites still held Jerusalem. Once the civil war had ended, the king marched against them. They despised him and ordered the maimed to go up on the wall and mock David, who already held the citadel. Scripture calls this the "stronghold". So he ordered that all the enemy be struck with javelins, according to the sentence God had pronounced from the beginning. That is also why he named Zion a city, meaning the upper city. Where it says "let him attack with a dagger", Symmachus has "whoever strikes a Jebusite and seizes the battlement." Aquila has "everyone striking a Jebusite, and he will reach into the water shaft." This shows that they had to strike hard, to the point of bloodshed. "And the Lord Almighty was with him." Let the heretics be ashamed, for this is often what [the Scriptures] called the divine Spirit. "Into the valley of the Titans." They used the names Giants and Titans for those whom the Hebrews call Rephaim. Hebron and Gath also had such men. Goliath was one of them, and David's champions [fought them], and Scripture admired their brave deeds. So probably an ancient battle against these men took place here, and the place was named for it. "And he stood against them near the place of weeping." Aquila has "opposite the pear trees." As [?] he spurs them on to valour, persuading them not to rely on their own strength but to wait for the divine [?]…

"And Uzzah and his brothers, sons of Abinadab." Some say that Uzzah was punished for rashness, because he tried to help the ark. The ark protected the whole people and had no need of help from anyone else. Josephus, however, says it was because Uzzah dared to touch the ark although he was not a Levite. Yet he was the son of Abinadab, who was of the [?Levitical] tribe. The people of Beth-shemesh had handed the ark over to Abinadab after the Philistines released it. For Scripture says, "He consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the covenant…"

[?] …himself, without using a cart. Instead he struck up music on instruments with the priests, as the law prescribed, and wore an extraordinary robe, that is, a many-colored one. The book of Chronicles shows this clearly: "For they carried the ark," it says, "as Moses commanded by the word of the Lord God of Israel, on poles, according to Scripture, on their shoulders." But if so, why did Uzzah alone suffer, and not all the Levites? And why did this happen not at the start, but only now, when he tried to steady it? Perhaps it was Uzzah who had proposed putting the ark on a cart. That is why he alone thought it right to help, and perhaps also why Scripture names him before his brothers. And he came to grief. When [David] saw what came of putting it on a cart, they were taught by the error [?] of God, or else he was unworthy in some other way [?]. "And she despised him in her heart." She thought it unfitting for a king to dance in public, for she did not know the goads of longing for God, which he revealed in his words to her. Scripture adds that she had no child. This shows the penalty for her mockery, and also ensured that no one from that seed would reign. The subjects would likely have preferred someone royal on both sides over the others. David danced, making his inner disposition public through the rhythmic movement of his body. At the same time he taught us not to be ashamed of the cross. Then dancing was a cause of reproach; now the cross is the [?]… [?] "…in your heart" [?]. The prophets did not foreknow everything, only what divine grace revealed to them. So Samuel did not know whom…
…he ought to anoint. So too [the prophet], speaking of the Shunammite's suffering, says, "And the Lord has hidden it from me." And now Nathan, having approved the…

"You shall not build me a house." He does not allow David to build a house of prayer, and so he teaches gentleness to those who would pray in it. They saw that the prophet was not permitted to build it because he had shed blood, even justly, and so they learned to keep their hands pure. On the whole, God preferred David. Before the coming of this grace, David lived in the old way with regard to women and practised it without fear. But he took great care over the worship prescribed by the law, over prayers and psalmody, over love for God, and over the salvation of the people. He was faithful to friends, grateful to benefactors and not harsh toward those who wronged him. He loved the poor as much as anyone ever has. For these reasons he is said to be after God's heart. Being mortal, he did err at times, and the Master rebuked him. But God did not turn away from a man who was good apart from a few things. As on a just scale, God found that his good deeds far outweighed his failings. "And it shall dwell by itself." Because it lived by the divine law, the people was set apart from the other nations. "And from the days when I appointed judges." In the time of the judges they were sometimes subject to the Ammonites and Moabites, and sometimes to the Midianites and Philistines. So he promised to keep their kingdom intact and to free them from these frequent changes…

"And I will establish his throne for ever." Similar things are said in the fourth [?] of Chronicles, and these passages clearly present the prophecy about Christ. That is why the Jews said to Christ, "We have heard from the law that the Christ remains for ever." God prepared the throne for him who built a house of living, spiritual stones into a holy priesthood, to the name of the Father. And God established his throne for ever. The Apostle, too, took from this passage the words in Hebrews, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me," together with what is said about the everlasting throne. Not all of this can fittingly be said of Solomon. How was his throne established for ever? If you say it was through the succession of his descendants, then this should have been said of David before Solomon. Second, how is this fulfilled: "The sons of Israel will remain many days without a king and without a ruler"? If it is true that the throne will not be established then, how then for ever…

But if these things are about Christ, how will these words fit: "And if his iniquity comes, I will rebuke him with the rod of men"? Perhaps it is like this: he took our sufferings upon himself, so he says that he himself suffered, hungered and thirsted. He is said to bear our weaknesses and to have put on the principalities and powers, so that he might later strip them off and triumph over them openly on the tree. So too in the twenty-first psalm: "Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions." And in the sixty-eighth: "Zeal for your house will consume me." He also says, "O God, you know my folly, and my offenses are not hidden from you." The words "And if his iniquity comes" should be read in the same way. Even here it does not say "If he does wrong," but "If his iniquity comes." But we who are his [?]…

"In all Judea he set up garrisons." Now the promise Isaac made to Jacob is fulfilled: "Be lord of your brother." For David struck Idumea and placed it under garrison. By "those set up" he means the guards stationed there, whom some now call "installed agents". "Over the records": Aquila has "recorder." "And Ahimelech son of Abiathar." They say this is a scribal error, since on the contrary Abiathar was the son…

"To prepare for the stranger." He calls the evil thought a stranger, because it attacks us from outside and is not in us by nature. "That the man who did this deserves death." This is hyperbole, but repaying fourfold is according to the law. "To be your wife." The text hints that God was more angry at the marriage than at the adultery that came before it. He committed the adultery stupefied by desire, but the marriage involved the consent of his reason. He should have mourned over the adultery and the murder, [but instead added] an unlawful marriage…

"And I will take your wives and give them to your neighbour." This is like the words "God gave them up to dishonourable passions," and it shows God's permission. Jacob did something similar. Against his will, his sons Simeon and Levi had destroyed Shechem, and he cursed them for it. Yet when he gave it to Joseph as an inheritance, he said, "which I took with my bow." He claimed as his own the deed of his sons, even though it was done against his will. "You shall not die." By the law he owed a double death, for adultery and for murder, but his confession of sin averted it. "You have provoked the Lord through the adversaries": Aquila says more clearly, "you have provoked the enemies of the Lord." Stripped of God's care, he made it possible for the Philistines to win and to grow arrogant against the God of all. Uriah was a proselyte, since God calls him a Hittite. "And your son who was born to you shall surely die." If he had lived, he would have been proof of the transgression. So God, caring for a pious king, removed this reproach. That is, the child of adultery. So great was the fruit of the repentance he had sown that the forefather of His own birth according to the flesh came from this very woman. "Jedidiah" [?]: Aquila has "for the Lord's sake" and Symmachus "for a king set apart." "And he sawed them with a saw." This was not an act of cruelty but a just punishment. For of the Israelites…

"And Jonadab was a very shrewd man." Yet the advice he gave was unlawful. So Scripture praises his wits, even though he used them badly, just as it calls the serpent most shrewd. And he paid the penalty for his bad advice: "For if you saw a thief," it says, "you ran with him, and you cast your lot with the adulterer." "A tunic reaching to the ankles": Symmachus has "sleeved", and Aquila has karpōtos, meaning one with "fruits" (karpoi) woven into it. People now call it embroidered. Josephus says it was one that reached down to the ankles. "To Talmai." He fled to his grandfather on his mother's side. His mother Maacah was the daughter of Talmai, who reigned over Geshur.

"And we will put him to death for the life of his brother." She is hinting at David. He neither punished Amnon nor relieved Absalom's dejection, and now that the deed could not be undone, he was angry to no purpose. "And let the king pass over this word." How can you, she says, save my son from slaughter without bringing back your own son? That, she says, will be the precedent for this. Otherwise the tribesmen will object, and they will have a reasonable pretext: your son's exile. So do not give the people of the Lord such a pretext for objecting. Then she consoles the king about the dead son. Water that is spilled cannot be gathered up again, and in the same way the dead man will not rise. Why, then, are you so determined to be deprived of the living one as well? "So as to bring your face around." She says it was not possible to plead with you directly. So he advised me to use this roundabout speech, so that you would see your own case in a made-up story of suffering. Then you would apply to yourself the remedy you were about to give me.

"Return the ark of God to the city." Being both pious and a prophet, he knew what had happened to the ark when it was taken out to punish the lawless. They were killed, and the ark was captured as spoil. With this in mind he thought it right to send it back. He could not carry around with him the law that accuses adulterers and murderers, of which he was guilty: "For you shall not kill the innocent and the righteous." But when, he says, the lawgiver cleanses the eye of my soul, then I will be able to see its beauty.

He means the Mount of Olives, from which Christ the Lord was taken up. And he worshipped God there, looking toward the tabernacle, as is likely, and toward the ark that lay in it. Hushai, David's chief companion. Some people disapprove of Hushai's lie. They do not realize that a lie told for a good purpose is equal to the truth. With good things and their opposites alike, we must look for the aim, and in this way we will find each one to be good or bad. Who would not condemn Herod's truthfulness, which led to the murder of the Baptist? Since he had sworn as he ought not to have, a lie would have been preferable to the slaughter. Here too, then, the pretense was not for gain of money or for harm to others, but for the life of a prophet and a pious king.

Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is yours. Some have blamed David for being too ready to believe. But it has been said [?] that the prophets do not know everything. And [Ziba] offered persuasive words and gifts, displaying his goodwill. But when David learned the truth, he divided the property between the two of them. He also cared for Mephibosheth again. When the Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's kin because of the famine, he did not hand over Mephibosheth, since he was keeping his covenant with Jonathan. And by reducing his property he brought down his [pride?], so that he would not dream of tyranny. Perhaps [?] he also accepted his defense, as a good man would. For he would not have made the man who lied against his master a sharer with him when he ought to have punished him. [?] Behold, my son, who came out of my belly [seeks my life]. This man, he says, had an old enmity against me, being of Saul's kin, and [it is natural] that he should take revenge on me now that he sees my own son plotting against me. It is, then, a divine sentence, bringing what was foretold to fulfillment. And one must endure, and turn aside the divine wrath by meekness. These things the divine man [said]. Yet neither Amnon's unlawful intercourse, nor Absalom's murder of his brother and his great madness against his father, were the work of God. Rather, David's house, stripped of divine care, was like a ship without a helmsman, and it took the [billows?] of wicked waves.

Such is all the counsel of Ahithophel, both to David and to Absalom. How did David use this man as a counselor, when he gave wicked counsel? It shows that he adapted himself to whoever he was with, and gave his counsel to suit the character of each. With the good man he concealed [his wickedness]. With the base man, who delighted in evil, he displayed his wickedness. And he offers to kill [David] [?], fearing lest [?]

[?] nature [should bring] both of them [together], and he should pay the penalty for his treachery. Yet he did not escape punishment. Having [armed?] a son against his father, he himself received [death?] at his own hands.

Note that here he calls Hushai the son of Archi, but in the title of the seventh psalm, the son of Jemini. Perhaps, then, since he displayed great valor and courage through his feigned friendship, he is called son of Jemini for this reason, that is, "son of the right hand"? David very wisely set a shrewd man against a shrewd man. For shrewdness is stronger than power, while power without shrewdness tends to destroy those who rely on it. And the Lord commanded that the good counsel of Ahithophel be frustrated. Divine Scripture taught that God worked together with Hushai. It calls "good" the counsel that served the tyranny. That is why David said in the Psalms: "Behold, he was in labor with iniquity; he conceived trouble and gave birth to iniquity. He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole he has made." And they dried [?] fruit-cakes. Aquila and Symmachus,

No heart will remain in us. Some read this as a question: "If you live, will we not all be of good courage?" [?] Others read it as a negation: "If you die," meaning, "We shall lose heart." And if some of us die, he says, the survivors are not enough to console us. They keep David from going out because they fear that something may happen to him, since the enemy would probably advance against him alone. At the same time they fear that if he wins he will take pity on the tyrant. So they say: "If we are defeated and flee, your life is consolation enough for us. But if anything happens to you, the disaster will fall on all of us. For you alone are worth ten thousand times as much as all of us." Symmachus shows this too when he says: "And you are as ten thousand of us." [For] he said: I have no son. Yet the writer said earlier that he had three sons and one daughter. But it is likely that he had children and that they died. Josephus said that he did this because children could not last long, whereas a building would preserve [his memory] better.

…having killed Absalom. For God himself got there first and hung him in the branches of the oak, to be tortured like a criminal. When Joab saw this, he left the father to show his kindness, while he himself lent God his right hand against Absalom and drove the darts into his utterly abominable heart. And the king wept. For he who had mourned Saul out of humanity, how could he not be overcome by nature in the case of his own son? He also laments, as a pious man, one who could no longer be healed through repentance.

If you will not be commander of the army for me. Although Joab had endured many dangers for David, David hated his boldness. He put up with him because of the goodwill Joab kept toward him, and also because he feared that Joab might plot some rebellion. But now, finding his opportunity, he promises the command to Amasa, whom Absalom had appointed general. Amasa too was David's nephew. When Joab learned of this, he killed him under a pretense of friendship.

Chapter [?]. And David grew weary. Being old, and having fought very many battles in the front line, his body gave out. But he was saved unexpectedly and escaped the hands of the giant. Scripture shows that people of that time used this name for those who were great in body and had irresistible strength, and not for the impious or the long-lived, as some have supposed.
The words of this song. After the wars he composed a hymn of victory to God. And he prophesies about Christ the Lord. Apart from a few details it is the same as the seventeenth [?] psalm.

The Spirit of the Lord spoke in me. Let the Jews be ashamed, who will not allow David to be called a prophet, though he so clearly foretold what concerns Christ and the faith of the Gentiles. For if the Spirit of God was in him, and the God of Jacob was pleased to speak in him and revealed to him the hidden things of wisdom, how is he not a prophet? And he would not drink it. For he had learned by experience how many calamities desire brings. He hung him on a tree. [?] One of the soldiers saw this and did not strike a blow against the man
caught by his hair [?], for he [respected] the king's command. [?]

Renowned among the three, more glorious than the two. Having praised the three, he says that Abishai was superior to the two but inferior to the first. For the first killed nine hundred in battle, while this one killed six hundred. He was first of the three not in deeds but in rank. Note that Benaiah son of Jehoiada was the king's nephew, for he called him a descendant of Jesse. And after speaking of his valor many times, he added that he was more glorious than the three, yet did not attain to the three. Though he fell short of the strength of the three, he was glorious because he had been entrusted with the king's guard. And David set him over his guard.

Saying: Go, number Israel. If God commanded it, how is David held to account for the census? We must understand here not words but God's permission. For God allowed him to follow this line of thought. Accordingly, in Chronicles it says: "And Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to number Israel." This is what the Hebrews call the adversary, the apostate. Since such reasoning was contrary to the divine promises, Scripture calls it by this name. And it did not say "against David" but "against Israel," on whom the punishment also fell. Scripture calls the devil the wrath of God. That is why in Chronicles it calls this wrath Satan. And if it was the wrath that spoke, and not God himself, then the wrath that spoke is something other than him. As here it says, "The wrath of the Lord incited," so there it says, "Satan incited," since the inciting is the cause of the sinning. The cause of sin, then, is the devil, who is named by both titles and who persuades the saints to commit sin, on which punishment follows. But how is it that David took the census and the people are punished? The people paid the penalty for their own lawlessness. They had deserted the pious king appointed by the God of all and sided with an impious and lawless son. Saul, who had been condemned and stripped of divine grace, they did not abandon until his death, even though David had been anointed by the prophet. But the man who had won countless blessings for them, who had broken the insolence of the Philistines and was a prophet, they not only abandoned but even took up arms against. Therefore they pay the penalty through David, against whom they had behaved so outrageously. Hence Scripture says that the wrath of the Lord was kindled against Israel, not against David. The census was the pretext for the punishment. Accordingly, he strikes only those who had revolted and does not touch those too old or too young for service at all. For he had to set the future in order beforehand and check the constant revolts in advance. And David, very piously, did not ask for the punishments in which, being king, he would probably have had an advantage. He himself would not have lacked food if there had been a famine, and with his fortifications he would easily have escaped his enemies. So he asks for something that no human influence can sway, entrusting himself, on equal terms with the others, to the verdict of the One who is greater.

[?] and of the nights to the days, it turns out that a twelfth part of the threatened punishment was brought upon the people. In this way God, who loves humanity, uses greater threats to frighten sinners, but inflicts punishments much smaller than the threats. There were one million three hundred thousand men, that is, of those of military age, not counting the too young and the too old, nor women, nor the Levites and the tribe of Benjamin, which was not numbered because the king repented. Yet only seventy thousand were taken, and they were not destroyed in an instant. The avenging angel did not need time, for in an instant he killed both the firstborn of the Egyptians and the hundred and eighty thousand Assyrians. So the time allowed was a mark of kindness, not of weakness. Some have interpreted the present passage allegorically, as follows. By divine wrath, death held sway over the people of the Lord until the hour of the midday meal, that is, from the beginning of the age until the time of the table, namely until the spiritual bread came down from heaven. Then God, moved to compassion, put an end to the destroyer and to death. Since the destroyer wished to lay his destructive hand once again on those who dwell in the holy [city], the Church, he is then commanded to refrain from the inhabitants of the Church who are made perfect through the living bread. "For glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." For the destroyer was not to prevail after the time of the holy table had been revealed, which the time of the meal hints at. The one who saved is Christ, understood as in the person of Christ [?], who offered himself for us and called the sin his own, though he knew no sin. For he takes away our sin, suffers for us, and as the good shepherd has laid down his life for the sheep. And in the literal history too, David, not knowing the cause, called what had happened his own sin [?]

to buy the threshing floor from you. The threshing floor is a type of the Church, through which death comes to an end. For it is the house of the life that is life by nature, that is, of Christ. Onto it are gathered, like sheaves of ears of grain, those who are cut off from the world through the word of the saints, so that they may be brought together into the courts above, as into the master's storehouse, after what is more worthless and superfluous, both in deed and in thought, has been put away. This is what is meant by the chaff. Therefore he says: "Lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for harvest. The reaper receives wages." And again: "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few," and what follows. And John says of Christ: "His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor thoroughly

and gather his wheat into the barn." ON THE THIRD [BOOK OF KINGDOMS]. [?] why "advanced in days" is said [?]; also, how "elder" and "old man" differ [?]. Elder and old man. And she was the king's bedfellow. They thought of the girl's youthful vigor, so that the living, warm flesh of youth might comfort David. It is the nature of clothing to preserve the body's warmth, but not to increase what it finds there, and something cold is of no help at all. But warm flesh passes on its heat to whatever can receive it. And Orneas son of Haggith. This is Adonijah, for he had two names. And sheep and lambs. Perhaps "sheep" means animals from the flock and from the herd of goats, while "lambs" means animals from the flock only, and of one age. Near Ain. He held the banquet by a spring that gushed up before the city, beside which a royal garden flourished. So Josephus said. Symmachus too translated "Ain" as "spring," just as the Syrian also calls it.

And Nathan came to Bathsheba. Some foolishly supposed that Nathan was offended at not being invited to the banquet, and that this is why he did these things. But the prophet knew God's decree, for God had made it known to the king through him: "You shall not build me a house; but behold, a son will be born to you, Solomon is his name; he will build a house for my name." Seeing Orneas seizing the kingdom against the divine will, he reminded the king of the divine prophecy through Bathsheba, and then went in and confirmed her words. And lambs and sheep. Here too it says these are different. And bring him down to Gihon. Gihon is the Nile, as Jeremiah says: "And now what have you to do with the road to Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon?" They also gave the name Gihon to Siloam. Either they called it so ironically, because it is very small, or because it too comes out of hidden underground channels, like the Nile. He observes an order, putting first Zadok the priest, then Nathan the prophet, and after them Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the general, who had slingers and archers, the Cherethites and the Pelethites. Above your name. They knew that no one who has a father's affection is jealous of his son. Such fathers pray to see their sons even more illustrious than themselves. So David was so delighted with what the officials said that, though old age kept him from rising, he worshipped God lying down, because God had brought his promises to fulfillment.

Chapter 2. And you shall be strong, and become a man of power. He says this as though it were up to Solomon to become a man. First the one who is to become a man is strengthened. To keep his way, and what follows, as far as "that you may understand." That is, do not dare to transgress even the least of what is written. That you may understand. For unless we hold to what is written, we do not understand what we are to do. And now you know what Joab did to me. How could he command his son to do what he himself had not done? He himself respected Joab as one who had shared so many dangers with him. At the same time he feared him, and said: "The sons of Zeruiah are too harsh for me." He also saw Joab helping Orneas set up his tyranny. So he feared that Joab might kill the young man, either while pretending to be well disposed, as he had done with Abner and Amasa, or even openly, as he destroyed [Absalom?]. And though he had pardoned Shimei, he now commanded his son to kill him, fearing his tyrannical and insolent character. As a prophet he knew that once Shimei found his opportunity he would not spare even his son. He who even

[?] so he urged him [to repay] this man's wickedness. And he was buried in the city of David. This is what Scripture calls Zion, which was the upper city. But now the whole of it is called Jerusalem. Josephus says that David was buried there, and the kings after him, and that the tomb is beside Siloam, shaped like a cave and displaying royal magnificence. He also said that Solomon buried much gold with him. For when the city was besieged by Antiochus son of Demetrius, Hyrcanus the high priest opened the tomb and took eighty [?]. David died at seventy years of age. He became king at thirty and reigned for forty years. And "he slept" is first used of David's death. You should consider whether these things were written on account of Christ, who lay down and slept like a lion and like a lion's whelp. That is why it is said: "I lay down and slept," and
