And he killed Orneas. Some are indignant with him for killing his brother. But human ways of life differ. Some practice the highest philosophy, others what is called civic virtue, and others pursue kingship or generalship. So each person must be judged by his way of life. Solomon did not have the perfection of a prophet or of a citizen, but the perfection proper to kings. From experience, then, he knew that Orneas was aiming at tyranny. At first he pardoned him, in case he should come to his senses. Now he killed him when he asked for his father's consort, since this was the road to tyranny and the beginning of civil wars. To Joab, into the tabernacle of the Lord. In accordance with the law he orders the murderer to be killed, though he had fled to the tabernacle of the Lord. As [chief priest?], in place of Abiathar. For Abiathar had shared in Orneas's tyranny, as Solomon's words also show. And besides, Solomon became the agent of the divine prophecy. For God had foretold to Eli, both through Samuel and through another prophet, the disgrace of his family. Understanding to Solomon, and much wisdom. It expressed wisdom by parallel terms [?]. For this reason it mentioned the wise men of old without naming them. And it put the Egyptians first, since everyone thought them wise. For as the Greeks have recorded, Pherecydes of Syros, Pythagoras of Samos, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae and Plato of Athens travelled to them to learn natural philosophy and a more exact theology. That is why Scripture says: "And Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians." Solomon surpassed them, having received wisdom as a gift from God. But Scripture joined blame to its praise, for he unlawfully married a foreign wife.

Chapter [?]. Over the burdens. He was in charge of those who carried stones and timber. In Chronicles these are called burden-bearers. And over the plinthion. By naming one part of the battle order it refers to the whole army. They also call this a plaision, meaning the square shape of the formation. This officer was the same as the one who is now called among the Romans the magister, the commander of the troops who guard the emperor. And the people burned incense on the high places. They did so not to idols but to God, though against the law, for he had commanded that sacrifice be offered in one place. But they were pardoned because they did not yet have a temple. This also explains what is recorded about the other kings: that they removed the groves and smashed the pillars of Baal, but did not remove the high places. Scripture says the same about Solomon, that he sacrificed on them, but not in the tabernacle before the ark. For if he had sacrificed to idols, God would not have appeared to him. And what you did not ask for I have given you. This agrees with: "Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you."

And Zadok and Abiathar were priests. Yet he had removed Abiathar, but from office, not from the priesthood. They held the priesthood not by appointment but by descent. For the king and his household. What was supplied for the king's table was consumed not only by servants but also by the soldiers on guard and the officials. And he was wiser than [Ethan?]. At that time there were some who were famous for wisdom. Ethan and Heman were among the psalm-singers who praised God with lyres, harps and cymbals. About the trees. He discoursed on the natures and powers of herbs, trees and animals. It is likely that the writers on medicine drew a great deal from these works.

And Pharaoh gave them. Having betrothed his daughter to Solomon, it says, he gave her the cities as a dowry. To anoint Solomon. It calls his appointment an anointing, for a foreigner did not anoint the king of Israel. As a friend of his father, then, he joined in approving his kingship. Mechir. Mechir means "measure." Others translated Bath as "batus." It is a measure of Palestine [?]

"Unhewn stones." He built the temple from stones of this kind: by divine providence he found stones that needed no iron to fit together with perfect exactness. With hewn stones, however, he built the enclosure wall of the sanctuary, the palace, the wall of the capital city, and the other [?] that [he wanted to be] stronger [?]

"Its length was forty cubits." A little later he also mentions another twenty cubits for the house of the Holy of Holies, so that the total comes to sixty cubits. The temple faced east, so that [?] when they prayed they would not worship the rising sun but the Lord of the sun. By "Elam" he means the porch. "Latticed, hidden windows." The temple had openings to let in light. These were wide on the inside but very narrow on the outside, and they were covered with pierced stones. This is what the text means: [?] for from outside. By "chambers" he means the small rooms that ran around the temple on every side. These held the temple together, kept any of the Levites from touching its walls, and served to store the vessels of the divine service. By "Dabeir" he means the Holy of Holies. "The lower side, five cubits." No one should be surprised that the rooms on the ground floor were five cubits wide, those on the second storey six cubits, and those on the third storey seven cubits. The walls were thicker at the bottom so that they could bear the weight of the building. As the walls narrowed in stages, a cubit was added to the rooms of the second storey and two cubits to those of the third. Josephus, however, says that the temple itself also had two storeys and that its whole height was a hundred and twenty cubits, as the book of Chronicles also shows. "And no iron tool was heard." The stones of the temple were in their natural state, but he ordered the stones of the enclosure to be hewn on the mountain and fitted to one another there. "And a winding stair to the middle." The wall was very thick, so it contained a spiral staircase. "To the second [?] and the third," since the temple had upper storeys. He covered it with cedar boards and covered the boards with gold [?]. By "bonds" he meant timber bands. He says that he set these bands at every five cubits of stonework. "And he made an altar in front of the Dabeir." The altar of incense stood in front of the veil, with the table on one side and the lampstand on the other. "The inner court." Just as the temple was divided in two,

so too were the open-air courts. Some of these were open to all the people, and others [?] to the priests and the Levites. A low parapet separated [?] from [?], so that those barred from the inner area could watch the offering of the sacrifices from outside. "Through three courses," he says, "they ran a band of cedar."
"And two capitals." That is, architraves. "And a cornice on both pillars." The

"The sea." This was a bronze basin in which the priests washed. He called it a sea because of its size. The sea was shaped like a hemisphere, ten cubits in diameter and thirty-three cubits in circumference, and a span thick. If the two spans, one on each side, are added to the diameter, the result is eleven cubits, and three times that makes thirty-three. "A lily blossom." The rim of the basin curved outward, imitating the petals of a lily. "Ten stands." The book of Chronicles called the stands basins, and Josephus called them bases. He says they were square and had wheels beneath them like the wheels of chariots. On top they had carved hands holding a ring shaped like a crown. "Ten cauldrons." These were basins set on the stands. In them they washed the sacrificial animals, their entrails and their feet, as Chronicles says. "And the three heaters." By "heaters" he means the vessels in which we usually heat water. "The holy things of David." These were the things he had dedicated from his wars.

"The house of the Forest of Lebanon." He made this the vestibule of the hall of judgment. It had 135 cedar pillars. That is probably why it was called the house of the Forest of Lebanon: its many cedar columns imitated the forest of Lebanon. "Forty-five, one row." It had three colonnades, and each had forty-five columns. The fourth colonnade was formed by the porch of the hall of judgment, which he calls [?]. The colonnades were joined to one another at their ends by [?]... "space facing space, three times." He called the colonnades "chambers."

"What you spoke with your mouth, you have also fulfilled with your hands." That is, you have brought what you said to completion. "Will God truly dwell with men on the earth?" He means: you, whose nature cannot be grasped, had a temple made by hands built, not because you are confined
[?] within it but because you make your own presence manifest in it. This is shown by the words, "that your eyes may be open toward this house day and

"And hear from heaven." In all these petitions he plainly says each time that God hears, not from the house on earth, but from heaven. He also admits that he built the temple, not for God himself, but for his name. He knew that God cannot be contained and that he fills all things. Isaiah too says: "Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me? says the Lord. Or what is the place of my rest?" "And he said he would dwell in thick darkness." David says, "Cloud and thick darkness surround him." And again: "And thick darkness was under his feet." And again: "And he made darkness his hiding place." The darkness and the thick gloom point to the invisibility of the divine nature. So he says that God, who set the sun in the heavens so that people might enjoy its light, himself said he would dwell in thick darkness. At the spiritual level this signifies that God is beyond comprehension. At the literal level it points to the temple, which had very [?] light openings, since it also had other small rooms all around it. That is why he says, "You said, 'Build me a house, a fitting house for yourself, to dwell in newness.'" God himself did not need such a building, but he ordered it to be built because people needed it. David handed over to Solomon the plan of the temple, the gold and silver, and the number of the vessels, as the book of Chronicles says: "For David gave everything to Solomon in writing from the hand of the Lord." It also says that the temple was decorated with many kinds of marble: "onyx stones, stones for setting, costly stones." And again: "precious stone, and Parian stones in abundance." "In the book of the song." As we have said, there were many prophetic books, and this will be clearly shown in Chronicles. "Seven days and seven days." He gathered the people at the Feast of Tabernacles. They held a festival for fourteen days: seven for the dedication and seven for Tabernacles. So by "the eighth day" he means the day after the last seven days.

...and they lie opposite the Axumites, with the sea between the two peoples. "A great quantity of hewn timber." This probably means timber that was smooth and free of knots. Josephus says it was pine, but not at all like the pines we have. He says it was whiter than fig wood, smoother, and harder. "And nablas and kinyras." Each of these has ten notes. They say the nabla is played with the fingers and the kinyra is struck with a plectrum. "And ships from Tarshish with gold." Here he used this name for a region of India. The translators of Ezekiel, however, used it for Carthage, the leading city of Libya.

"She burned incense and sacrificed to their idols." The meaning is clear: he built the shrines for them, and they worshipped the idols. "I will take it out of your son's hand." He means: you have your father's merit to help you, but your son will be stripped of his father's help. "I will give one sceptre to your son." He means: I will add Benjamin to the tribe of Judah. He had very good reason to join these two tribes, for the royal line belonged to the tribe of Judah, and the divine temple to that of

"So that my will may be with my servant David." He means: I foresaw David's virtue from the beginning, so I chose him and was well pleased with him. This is what he calls his "will." I appointed him and his descendants to reign over Jerusalem, where I wished my name to be revered. "Forty years." But Josephus says that Solomon reigned eighty years and died at the age of ninety-four.

"My littleness is thicker than my father's loins." Chronicles puts it more clearly: "My little finger is thicker than my father's loins." The Syriac version and Josephus also render it this way. "For the turn of events was from the Lord." This is like "The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart." When God abandons someone, that person drifts like a ship without a helmsman. By speaking those foolish words, Rehoboam caused God's decree to be fulfilled. "Daughter of Anan, son of Nahash, king of the Ammonites." This is enough to put the Jewish kingdom to shame. They pride themselves on their noble descent and call those from the nations who have believed in the Saviour foreigners, yet even their royal line turns out to be of foreign stock. "And Jeroboam came out of Egypt." The same things twice

[?]: he is often forced to repeat himself because he is writing about two divided kingdoms. Sometimes, after telling a story about one kingdom, he moves on to the other and has to take up again what he has already said in order to keep the sequence of events. "To Shemaiah the Salamite." How can the text say above that Ahijah the Shilonite tore his cloak and gave ten pieces to Jeroboam, but here that it was Shemaiah the Salamite? Both things happened. The first happened while Solomon was still alive, and that is why Jeroboam fled to Egypt full of hope. The second happened after his return from there and reminded him of the divine prophecy, so that, knowing that his kingdom was a gift from God, he would govern it according to the divine laws. "He set one in Bethel and the other in Dan." [?] These marked the borders of the kingdom of the ten tribes: Bethel in the south and Dan in the north. His purpose was that people would go to one or the other, find the trip easy because the places were nearby, and gladly accept not having to travel to the capital. "Like the feast held in Judah." On the fifteenth [?]... the feast according to the law of Tabernacles. In this way [?] he held the festival.

"And another old prophet." Some people think he was a false prophet. Perhaps, though, he was a prophet of God who told lies to the man of God, not to harm him but to share in his blessing. That is why God foretold to the man of God through him what would happen. He also believed what had been prophesied about Josiah and gave orders to be buried with the man of God. "And he lied to him." Perhaps it is in this respect that he was a false prophet, since he invented divine words for the sake of the blessing

"And it killed him." The story teaches that "the mighty will be mightily tested." The man who had heard the divine voice ought not to have been swayed by a man in any way. He should have waited for another word from God releasing him from what God had commanded. This punishment probably also served to confirm the prophecy about the divine altar. If eating food was punished so severely as a transgression, how much more would preferring idols to the Creator be [?]... images? The prophet's [?] reveals the resurrection of the dead. For the one who did not give him over [?] to the beast while he lived, and who thought him worthy of honour [?] after his death, [preserved] not his soul but only his body. This clearly shows that

the body is the soul's instrument, through which it served the Creator [?]. Not every prophet, however, is called [?] a "man of God," but only those who have attained perfect virtue, such as Moses, Elijah and anyone like them. So it shows

"And there was a conspiracy in the..." In the same way Jezebel, when she learned of Joram's death and Jehu's accession, cried out, "Conspiracy! Conspiracy!" That is, revolt and usurpation. "Into the Thekoue." In the Lexicon of Hebrew Names this is also interpreted as "trumpet blast." From what Chronicles seems to indicate, he says, these [weapons] were given to those who guarded the gates of the palace. When the king went out, some of them went ahead of him and others ran alongside. When they reached the temple, the guards coming back from the temple met them and took the weapons from them. Holding these, they stood in front of the temple gate, so that the weapons stayed outside the doors while those who had carried them worshipped God with the king. It is likely that a room was also built in front of the doors where the armed men could leave their weapons. ... seemed ... some of the bodyguards went ahead to worship and waited in front of the temple, watching for the king's arrival. They met those escorting him before they arrived, laid hands on them and disarmed them as they went in with the king, and kept the weapons until he came out again.

"For the Lord had given David a remnant in Jerusalem." He gave the reason why these kings, though impious, still reigned: they survived because of their ancestor. The book of Chronicles, however, praised Abijah's early actions, though it condemned his later ones, in agreement with this passage. "But he did not remove the high places." These were altars dedicated to God on the high places. "Come, break your covenant." He abandoned God and sought an alliance with the Syrians. "Asa did evil in the sight of the Lord." Chronicles is clearer: "In his illness," it says, "he did not seek the Lord, but the physicians." By "physicians" it means those who used incantations and sorcery. Or perhaps it means that he put all his trust in physicians and had no hope in God. Both medical skill and healing herbs come from God. When they are joined with faith in him, they serve those who cleave to him well, but without that faith they are useless.

"And Zimri went in and struck him down." God the Master punishes the wicked by means of one another. He hands the wicked over to someone more wicked, using them as his executioners. "From the owner of the hill of Somoron." The hill was called Somoron after Shemer, and the city was named after the hill:

Samaria, which is now called Sebaste. [?] For the saints too, the demons who come to wrestle with them become a source of spiritual food: they strengthen their hearts and train their spiritual condition. Solid food, the food of athletes, belongs to these. This condition comes to us after many bouts [?]. "To Zarephath of Sidon." And why to a foreign woman? [?] This too has the same reason. He had forbidden mixing with foreigners because of the weakness of the Jews. He would have allowed it if they had been steadfast enough to benefit those people, as the prophet Elijah did. In the law he gives this as the reason for keeping apart: so that through intermarriage their sons or daughters of Israel would not go whoring after the foreigners' gods. He also wanted [?] to show Elijah by deeds how the people were wasting away. First he led him to a brook and made it dry up, then to a widow who had food for one day.

She is also a type of the Church from the nations. She faithfully welcomed the one whom the Israelites were persecuting, just as the Church welcomed the apostles. "As the Lord your God lives." How admirable her gentleness! Amid such misfortunes she was not annoyed at being asked for food. She only pointed out her extreme poverty, then accepted the promise in faith and brought the food. And she did this without knowing who the man was, for she was a foreigner and had never seen prophetic power at work. "What have I to do with you, man of God?" The prophet had plenty to eat and forgot the misfortune of everyone else. That is why the Master turned the widow's laments against him. He himself recognized the cause, for he says, "Alas, Lord, witness of the widow," and so on. The widow's words are also admirable. She says, "Your light has exposed my hidden sins." She did not treat his arrival as a bad omen, as a foreigner would, but blamed it on her own sins. This shows how much she had already gained from the prophet's teaching. Perhaps the child died for her sake, so that by seeing a resurrection beyond the power of nature she would receive a firm faith. "And he breathed on the boy three times." After praying, he breathed on the boy three times and brought him back to life. The number points to the Trinity whom we worship, and the breathing points to the creation of the soul at the beginning. The prophet, however, did not create another soul by breathing. He brought back the soul that had been separated from the body.

Chapter 18 [?]. "Go and show yourself to Ahab." God loves humankind. He saw the human race perishing and saw that the prophet would not ask for mercy. He wanted to have pity on the people, but he would not revoke the prophet's sentence against the prophet's will. So the Master comes as an envoy to his servant, the Creator to the clay, and persuades the tongue that had bound the clouds to release their birth pangs. "If there is a nation or kingdom." The prophet had said to Ahab, "As the Lord my God lives, there will be no rain these years except by the word of my mouth." Ahab had found out that these words were true, so he naturally searched for the man who had bound the rain, either to make him release it or to kill him if he refused. "And the Spirit of the Lord will carry you off." These are the words of a man who studied divine things and knew the power of the divine Spirit. "On both hams." They both worshipped God and served idols. He means: God does not want the so-called gods to be honoured, and they in turn do not want the true God to be honoured. By doing both, you keep faith with neither.

"And let them choose one place for themselves." Why did he let the priests of Baal choose the fat bull and offer their sacrifice first? Clearly because the true God needs none of these things. But they would have claimed that Baal was angry at not being given first place and so did not accept the

"And he built the stones." How could Elijah build an altar on Carmel, when the law commands that worship be offered in one place? "The law is not laid down for the righteous," as the divine Apostle says, "but for the lawless and disobedient." That is what the Israelites were. If they had been given permission to sacrifice anywhere, they would have worshipped demons as well. The prophet wanted to show both the power of God and the weakness of the demons. With the kingdom divided, he could not bring the people who were there to the temple in Jerusalem, so he had no choice but to go to Carmel, where they used to hold most of their

"He made a trench." Josephus calls it a cistern. "Do it a third time." Here again he points to the number of the Trinity whom we worship. "And the fire licked up the stones and the dust." This was so that those impious men would not desecrate the divine altar by offering sacrifices on it to demons.

"And Elijah was afraid." How could he be afraid when he had such power? Because he was not only a prophet but also a man. Besides, the fear was part of God's plan. Grace allowed his nature to give way to fear so that the greatness of his miracles would not make him proud and he would recognize his own weakness. "Behold, the Lord will pass by." He taught Elijah that he had chosen to govern the human race with gentleness and patience. It would have been easy for him to send thunderbolts, shake the earth, turn it into a ready-made grave for the impious, and destroy everything with violent winds. "But patience is dear to me," he says. It is human wickedness that draws down each of the other things. Elijah was taught, and through him all of us, that the God of the Old Testament is not fire. Nor is he a light breeze, but he is said to be present in a light breeze. He had appeared to the Israelites in thick darkness and fire, but he found Elijah able to grasp higher things. So he led him up to the idea of the incorporeal, from earthquake, wind and fire to a light breeze. This comes close to the Saviour's saying, "God is spirit." "And he threw his mantle over him." Why did he anoint only the prophet, when he had been commanded to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha? [?] So he anointed him, and of the spiritual
[?] …with the grace he imparted to him, he also anointed the others. For having received the prophetic grace from him, he brought the anointing to them and imparted to them the royal grace.

"Naboth blessed God." He said this euphemistically in place of "blasphemed." She ordered the fast to be held so as to show by it that the murder was just. For the same reason she ordered that he be granted his customary honour and preside over the others, and only then face the charge. "He tore his garments." Being fickle, Ahab was always easily swayed; that is how Jezebel brought him to this impiety. This is why the history says, "Ahab sold himself for nothing to do evil in the sight of the Lord, as Jezebel turned him aside," and what follows. So, although he had coveted the vineyard, he grieved over Naboth's death. "And all that the Amorite did." Here it does not mean that particular [?] nation, but all the Canaanites; for in the Hebrew language "Amorite" also means "one who dwells." The God who loves humankind threatened total destruction because of the bloodguilt, but because of the lament over the murder, a postponement of the punishment

"If the dust of Samaria will suffice for handfuls." They said this as a threat of siege mounds. "Have you seen all this noise?" He fittingly called the bluster of their threatening words by this name, for it was swiftly dispersed by the divine influence. "By the young men of the governors of the provinces." "I have no need of a multitude," he says. "With a few youths, inexperienced in war, I will destroy this enormous army." There were, it says, two hundred and thirty-two of them, and through them the almighty Lord destroyed the army of thirty-two kings. "The God of Israel is a god of the mountains." Since they supposed their own gods to be of this kind, they thought that the true God, the creator of all things, was also a local god. But he showed his strength both to his own people and to foreigners. For when the battle was joined on the plain, Israel struck down a hundred and twenty thousand of the enemy. And so that they too might learn that the blow was sent by God, when the survivors took refuge in the city of Aphek, the wall fell and buried two hundred and seventy thousand. "By the word of the Lord, strike me." "It is not I who command you," he says, "but the Spirit within me." That is why he brought death by the lion on the man who refused. "And he struck." That is, he wounded him.

"And he bound his eyes with a bandage." The prophets use parables to deliver the divine predictions, so that those who hear these words, not realizing that they are passing sentence on themselves, may judge justly. For we see sin one way in ourselves and another way in others. Nathan did this to David, and now the prophet does it here. "Because you let go a man doomed to destruction." Ahab paid the penalty for unjust kindness, for kindness must keep to justice. But he, who had treated the prophets with cruelty, wanting to wipe them all out and killing all those he caught [?], showed gentleness toward the enemy of Israel. What follows bears witness that he sinned a great deal through the pliability of his mind. "To his house, confounded." Having had experience of the divine predictions (for he had twice won victories as the oracles said), he feared the threat delivered to him. But he soon went back to his own impiety.

"As you are, so am I." "The same as you [?]," he says. "As you take the field, so do I; your people fight, and so do mine." Scripture showed his [?] piety, even though his friendship and kinship with Ahab marred it, as in Chronicles. "Go up, and the Lord will give success." He waited to be put on oath, and only then told the truth. For since Ahab supposed that the prophet foretold [unwelcome things?] out of hatred, he first said what Ahab wanted, and then [?] made known the divine message. "Like sheep that have no shepherd." He shows [?] by this that it is the king's wickedness that brings about the defeat; for if they had had a pious shepherd, they would have defeated the enemy decisively. "Does he not prophesy good things for me…" [?] Josephus said that Micaiah was [?] the one who had earlier used the bandage and foretold the grievous things to Ahab, inferring this from Ahab's saying, "I hate him, because he speaks no good of me, but only evil." "And the Lord said, Who will deceive Ahab?" This is a personification teaching the divine permission. [?] …permitted Ahab to be deceived, saying through the prophet [?]… "Let each return to his house in peace." [?] By these words, then, the prophet taught that the spirit of deceit, using impious men as its instruments, falsely promises victory. This happens with God's permission.

For though he could have prevented it, he did not, since Ahab was unworthy of the divine care. Similar to this is what Paul says: "God will send a working of error on those who did not accept the truth." Visions are interpretations of God's will: they do not show him as he is, but portray God's dispensations in bodily forms and human words, as God himself says: "I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented." He does not himself appear, but multiplies visions. And he shows the prophets a likeness: of kingship, when they see him seated on a throne with the heavenly host around him; of judgment, when they see him white-haired and clothed in white garments, because judgment is at once wise and pure. Zechariah too sees winds speaking with a human voice: "Let us go about the earth," they say, "and behold, all the earth is inhabited." For just as painters represent war and peace, victory and friendship, and all such things in the form of human bodies, showing their meaning more vividly through such likenesses, in the same way the Holy Spirit portrays through visions to prophets and apostles the will of God, his glory, his dispensation, the curse on perjurers, and certain other things, animate or inanimate; and what God wills to accomplish and the powers under him carry out; or what the devil dares to plot and God permits, as in the case of Job. For visions, and the words spoken in visions, are part of God's condescension. The Holy Spirit is not a dove; nor shall we understand "who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us" just as it is stated, as though God were in a place and needed the intercession of the Only-begotten on our behalf. By the same reasoning, the visions and voices of the prophets were not what they appeared to be either. They signified God's will or his permission, the obedience of those who obey and the attempts of those who dare. So it was, for instance, with the spirit that lied through the mouth of the false prophets, God permitting it; and with the devil who tempted Job, God not preventing him. Through this Scripture taught us that he belongs to God's creation and dominion, standing before the Master of all not by obedience of will but as a consequence of his created nature: estranged in will, yet God's in his substance [?]. "And Jehoshaphat king of Judah with him." [?] …of the discourse against the Manichaeans. [?] Theodoret [?]

[?] …set out with Ahab, doing something unworthy of his own piety. For after asking for a prophet, sending away the false prophets and learning from Micaiah what should be done, he put friendship ahead of piety. Yet because of his other virtue he enjoyed God's care. "And the prostitutes bathed in his blood." The prostitutes bathed at dawn as was their custom. They did not deliberately mean to bathe in the blood, but in the spring water as they usually did; this, however, was stained with blood. And so, in human terms, the punishment seemed more bitter. Some, thinking this unworthy of being recorded in divine Scripture, said that all who took part in the same practice saw it and from then on stopped to some extent. Even if they did not at once cast off the habit itself, in this sense they bathed in his blood, since Ahab's death became their cleansing: it was seen as a check on their licentiousness. So too, "when a wicked man is punished, the innocent becomes wiser," as it says in Proverbs; so too, according to David, "the righteous will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner."

ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS. [?] …my [?], because of the daughters of the Canaanites; that is: And David, "I did not loathe wickedness" [?], that is, "Not" [?]… [?] For they deified not only the largest of animals but also the smallest, even those full of loathsomeness [?]. For what is more disgusting than a fly? Yet, abandoning the God of all, they consulted its image about life. One can learn, however, from what Eusebius quotes from Philo at the beginning of the Preparation for the Gospel, that it was a demon; he says this:

"Fire will come down from heaven." Those who accuse the prophet of cruelty in the matter of the captains of fifty are, without realizing it, blaspheming against God, who sent the fire. For we must recognize the justice of the divine dispensation, and that God both punishes and in turn does good with justice. The captains of fifty and their followers clearly agreed with the purpose of the one who sent them. The third, who approached with reasonableness and faith, having learned the prophet's power by experience, is saved. Some say that they came with heavy mockery, calling the righteous man and ordering him to come down to them. So instead of him, fire came down and burned up the impious, to teach that one must not ridicule and make sport of the righteous.

"Because he had no son." By law a son always succeeded his father on the throne; but if the one who died was childless, the eldest of his brothers did. So the kingship of David passed down through sons until the captivity. But when Jeconiah was taken captive before he had children, Mattaniah, also called Zedekiah, took the throne, being his uncle on his father's side [?]. "And fifty men of the sons of the prophets." It is an idiom of Hebrew, and also of Syriac, [?] to say "sons of prophets" and "sons of men" for prophets and men, as in: "Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?" and "In your greatness you have taken great care of the sons of men." There were many prophets, as the text has shown. "You have asked a hard thing." He says this not because he begrudges his disciple the grace, but out of concern for other people. For since he had chastised the impious people for three years and six months, and it was necessary that the one inheriting a double grace [?]… the punishment by famine, out of compassion he said, "You have asked a hard thing." We learn this from the history too, for the punishment of famine was brought on the people for seven years. "The chariot of Israel and its horseman." The kings of other nations went to battle with horses and chariots. For this reason he called the great Elijah the chariot and horseman of Israel, as one able even on his own to overcome the enemy and win favour for his people. "Where now is the God of Elijah, Aphpho?" Imitating his teacher, he struck the water of the Jordan with the mantle without saying anything. He thought the mantle sufficient to work the miracle, but when the water did not
[?] …yield, he calls on his teacher's God, who is invisible and inaccessible to human beings. For the other translators render "Aphpho" as "the hidden one." "Sons of power." Powerful, if

"And he cursed them in the name of the Lord." Through the punishment he became a benefactor both to them and to their parents: to the children by stopping a wickedness that would have grown with time, and to the parents by teaching them not to bring up their children like this, but in the fear of God and in reverence for the righteous. And he who did not spare even children taught the grown men a still sterner lesson. In any case, God's exact judgment took away those children whom he knew would turn out worse, and through their removal it instructed those who were not like them. That God avenges the saints

"Who poured water on Elijah's hands." They say this as praise, so great was their admiration for the great prophet. "Has the Lord not called these three kings?" Necessity makes even the bold reasonable. "Bring me someone who plays the harp." David, who had been granted both the prophetic and the royal grace, also wisely ordered the priestly liturgy. He commanded the priests to use trumpets, according to the law of Moses, and the Levites lyres, harps, cymbals and the other instruments. They used David's spiritual melody. The prophet ordered one of these to be summoned. While he played, the grace of the Spirit, which he calls the hand of the Lord, indicated what should be done.

"And you know that he was a servant of the Lord." Some say that this is Obadiah, Ahab's steward, who hid a hundred men indoors and fed them with bread and water; it was on their account that he dealt with a lender. "Is there anything you would like said to the king?" [?] Though he was able to provide her with divine help, he also wants to grant her human care. "No; I live among my own people." "I enjoy a quiet life," she says, "and live in peace; I cannot bear to have a dispute with anyone." So too, when the Holy Spirit cuts away worldly attachments, it makes every soul fruitful, even one that was barren.

"At this season, about this time [?]." The God of all said this to the patriarch: "At this season I will come, and Sarah will have a son." By what he said, then, the prophet shows that the Lord of all was speaking through him. That is why he also gave the promise categorically. "And she laid him on the bed of the man of God." Knowing the prophet's power, she hoped that the dead child would rise. "And she said, Peace." "I want to greet him." "Peace to you" means "Are you well? Are you in good health?" "And the Lord has hidden it from me." For the prophets did not know everything, but only what divine grace revealed to them. "If you meet anyone, do not greet him." He knew his love of honour, and vainglory hinders the working of miracles. "And he put his face on his face." So that the dead might share in the life of the living, the spiritual grace, clearly, supplying the life. [?] "He breathed into," they translated. "And he breathed upon him." The others, [?]. "Arioth." The others, [?]. "Take flour and throw it into the pot." It was not the nature of the flour that blunted the poison's power but the prophet's grace, just as it was not salt that changed the barrenness of the spring.

"Wash seven times in the Jordan." He would not consent to see him, since he was a leper, because he lived under the law. He prescribes the remedy at hand. For leprosy belonged to the body, which is composed of four elements, and the present life revolves in cycles of seven days. But the cleansing of the soul is accomplished according to the number of the Holy Trinity. "And Naaman was angry." He did not understand that John

[?] …the unclean, and healing. The prophet's task was to send him to the one who heals. But to lay on a hand and cleanse was the work of my Lord Jesus alone, who said only this to the man who believed: "I will; be cleansed." For along with the word he also touched him, and he was cleansed of his leprosy. "And he would not take it." The prophet preferred much-coveted poverty to all wealth, anticipating the law of the Gospel: "Freely you have received, freely give."
"And in this matter may the Lord pardon me." "I ask forgiveness," he says, "because royal necessity compels me to go in to the falsely named god."

"Alas, Lord, and it was borrowed." The words are an invocation, not a blasphemy, as also in David: "O Lord, save now; O Lord, prosper now." Through his actions the prophet Elisha showed that the solid word of God, which we carelessly lost and cannot find, we shall recover again through the dispensation of the wood. That the word of God resembles an axe, John the Baptist says of it: "Already the axe is laid at the root of the trees." And Jeremiah says: "The word of the Lord is like an axe splitting rock." This word, then, hidden from us, the dispensation of the wood has revealed. For since we lost it through wood, through wood we have received it back, as he shows in it the height and length and breadth and depth. For by the divine stretching out of his hands he gathered the two peoples into one head, the Father; for there is one God, who is over all and through all and in all. "Phelmouni." As one might say, "to such-and-such a place"

"And let them be sent back to their master." "If they are slaughtered," he says, "the greatness of the miracle will not be known; but if they go back to the one who sent them, he too will learn the power of our God." "Doves' dung." The straits of the siege led them to use it instead of salt.

"If the head of Elisha stays on him." When he ought to have begged the prophet to intercede with God for them, he threatened to kill him, as if the prophet were deliberately ignoring how extreme the disaster was. But he immediately repented and ran to stop the murder. This is what is shown by "Is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?"

"And she lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines." So the famine did not cover the whole land; [?] … Israel [?] was being chastised by [plagues?] for its impiety after so much care. The double portion of the prophet's grace is shown by the doubled length of the famine. "And Elisha came to Damascus." What Elijah, taken up before he could do it, had been commanded by God to do (anoint Hazael over Syria and Jehu over Israel), Elisha now comes to do, intending first to anoint Hazael. "And tell him, You will surely live." Do not reveal to him the

"And he spread it over his face, and he died." For he was, Josephus says, impious and bloodthirsty. It was he who had said, "The God of Israel is a god of the mountains"; and after being spared by Ahab, he proved ungrateful to his benefactor. See the outcome of a bad marriage alliance: Jehoram, son of the pious Jehoshaphat, was turned to impiety by his wife, the daughter of Ahab. "And he fell upon Edom." The king of the tribe of Judah ruled over the Idumeans. But Isaac had foretold concerning Edom: "There will come a time when you will break and loose his yoke from your neck." For now, even though they were defeated, they would no longer endure being ruled.

"And take the flask of oil." He anointed Jehu through another prophet, for it was expedient that this be done secretly, so that Joram might be killed swiftly. If he had found out in advance, many would inevitably have fallen in battle. "And flee, and do not wait." So that he would not be caught and put in danger. For God wants us to use human prudence as well; those honoured with reason ought to use reason as the situation requires. "Why did this madman come to you?" Being impious, they insulted God's servants and called their boldness of speech madness. Jehu called him a babbler not as one speaking drunkenly [?], but to escape notice

"Arameans." He called the Syrians by this name, for "Arama" means the Syrians, and the other translators rendered it the same way. "And the driving is like the driving of Jehu." The watchman, seeing from far off that those who had been sent had not returned and that the leader of the troop looked like Jehu (for his bearing showed it), reported what he had seen. Some copies, however, read: "And the one driving Jehu was God."

"Behold, I conspired." "I," he says, "wanting to seize power, killed Joram. But his brothers, seventy in number—who killed them? Was it not the wrath of [God's] will, making use of his own closest servants?" The predictions of the prophets are therefore not false. "And all his familiars." The diviners, those who thought they knew the future. For just as they called the prophets seers and beholders, so they called these too, as supposedly knowing future and hidden things. "And he found Jehonadab." He was a pious man himself, and so was his family; for they lived continually in tents [?]… [?] 3 Kings [?] 28.

[?] …living [in tents] and abstaining from drinking wine. The prophet Jeremiah also mentions them with praise. “And he blessed him” means “he greeted him.” “And I will serve him much.” We must look at the purpose, even if the words are blameworthy. He said this so that no one would escape. He sent away the priests of God, on the pretext that they were unworthy, taking care that they should not come to harm. “On the left of Baal [?].” This is what he called the precinct of Baal.

“And Ahaziah went against Hazael.” He went because he was Ahab's son-in-law. “And she destroyed all the royal seed.” Being impious herself, and wishing to strengthen [?] impiety among her subjects, she wanted to wipe out the royal line entirely, since it was pious. But God, who directs all things wisely, had arranged beforehand that the priestly tribe should again be joined with the royal one, and that Jehoiada, a most wise priest, should marry Jehosheba, the daughter of Joram, so that a spark of the royal line might be kept alive. For she stole away her nephew Joash, whom the wise priest restored to the kingdom after the sixth year. “The Chorri and the Rasim.” These are the runners and the guards. Some say shield-bearers and spear-bearers. By “those who run alongside” he means those who go before the king. He divided them into three groups. Some he ordered to guard the king's house, others the entrance of the temple, and others the other gate. “Messae.” The other translators rendered “Messae” as “from destruction.” It means that no damage [?] was to be done in the house of God. “Two hands among you” means “you are whole and sound, and able to guard both the house of God and the house of the king.” “Whoever enters into the Sederoth shall die.” In Chronicles it says, “And whoever enters the house shall die.” Josephus says the same. “From the right shoulder of the house.” This shows that the Levites formed a crescent shape with its horns joined to the house, and guarded the king, who stood in the middle. Outside, the armed troops surrounded them,

…as the other translators rendered it elsewhere. He handed down to them rules and laws for serving the Lord. And a good teacher is truly a light. While he lived, they worshiped God. Yet even so they fell short, since they sacrificed to God on the high places and not according to the law of God, as the law commanded.

CHAPTER 11. “The silver of a man's valuation.” In Deuteronomy [?] he had said how many shekels people who offer God a price for themselves ought to give. Joash now ordered the priests to collect this silver and to repair the damaged parts of the temple, since the wood and stones were decaying. This is what “bedek” means, which Chronicles calls “to restore the house of the Lord” and again “to repair the house of the Lord” [?]. “And the Lord repented and had compassion on them.” He calls the change from misfortune to good fortune “repentance.” “Take a bow and arrows.” People did not trust words as much as predictions made through actions. He supposed that the king would of his own accord shoot many arrows, and so after the first was shot he said, “An arrow of salvation,” and the rest. But when the king shot only three, he was vexed, because Syria would be defeated three times but would not suffer total destruction. CHAPTER 14 [?]. “The thistle that is in Lebanon.” Amaziah had defeated the Idumeans in war, and he hoped to conquer the ten tribes as well. So he challenged the king of Israel to battle. The king replied with the proverb, likening himself to the cedar and Amaziah to the thistle. “And the sons of the mixtures of abominations.” That is, the priests of the falsely named gods. The phrase points to how disorderly a crowd they were. “Elath.” This is the city now called Aila, which lies at the mouth of the Arabian Gulf, the sea they call the Red Sea.

CHAPTER 16 [?]. “And he made his sons pass through fire.” This seems to point to a form of error that has survived down to our own time. In some cities, once a year, people have seen bonfires lit in the squares, and some people leaping and jumping over them, not only boys but grown men as well. Mothers also carry their infants through the flames, supposedly to avert evil and for purification. Josephus says that Ahaz also offered one of his sons as a whole burnt offering to Baal. “And he saw the altar.” It seems that he did this not for the God of

the universe but for some idol. Chronicles hints at this when it says, “And Ahaz departed still further from the Lord,” and he said, “I will seek the gods of Damascus, who are striking me,” and the rest. “And the bronze altar.” The one that he made

“The seat of the Sabbaths.” There was a place in front of the temple where the king sat before the time of the sacrifices, or after them. He now moved it inside the temple, and he moved the door of the palace so that the passage ran through the sacred precincts, and this too was impious. He did this, supposedly, so that if the palace was besieged he could safely enter the temple through a connecting entrance. This is what “because of the king of Assyria” indicates. “Pillars and groves.” Everywhere the other translators render “grove” as Ashtaroth. This means Astarte, that is, Aphrodite. He says that altars were built to demons in every place, not only in cities and villages but also in the towers along the roads, where a few men used to keep watch with signal fires. Here he called the precincts of the demons “high places.” “And they made partners.” He seems to use this name for their alliance with the nations and for all who taught them impiety, as he hints next. “And they made an ephod,” the object used for divinatory predictions. “And Judah too.” So Israel did not fall into impiety because the kingdom was divided, as one might say, or because it was far from Jerusalem, since Judah did the same. “And Israel was carried away from its land to Assyria until this day.” This also shows that the writer lived later and took his history from the prophets, who recorded the events of each period. He also clearly explained the origin of the present-day Samaritans and how they came to keep the law of Moses out of necessity. “They did not know the law of the God of the land.” For they supposed that the Maker of the universe was merely a local god.

“The bronze serpent that Moses made.” It was made not to be worshiped but to prefigure the saving passion. Yet the people, he says, kept burning incense to it. “And he called it Nehushtan.” In the interpretation of Hebrew names this is given as “bronze.” I think this is why the Ophites (a most impious heresy) are called Esthenes. “At the end of three years.” The siege of Samaria lasted three full years.

…when he called him in against the Syrians, he promised to pay tribute, and he went on paying it. Hezekiah, however, did not pay the tribute imposed on him, but when he saw the army he promised to give it. “The doors of the temple of the Lord.” The royal treasuries were not enough, so out of necessity he turned to the sacred ones, as was customary, to keep the enemy from burning both the temple and the city. After such a need they used to refill the treasuries from the spoils of war. But this time he even melted down the golden doors that he had made, and their doorposts. “Did he not remove his high places?” The writer shows again that they called “high places” not only the precincts of demons but also the altars set up to the God of the universe in high places. “And he said to Judah and Jerusalem…” The Rabshakeh said these things. He was probably a Hebrew who had either deserted to the Assyrians or been enslaved, and after he had shown them his loyalty they entrusted him with the army. He spoke in Hebrew and so made the

“For the children have come to the birth pangs.” We are burning with anger, he says, because we have heard those unspeakable blasphemies. But we are unable to punish those impious men. So we beseech God, who heard those blasphemies, to teach these unholy men that there is not one

“Behold, I will put a spirit in him.” I think this means cowardice. The divine Apostle used the word in the same way: “For he did not give us a spirit of cowardice.” “And Sennacherib departed.” Sennacherib escaped death at that time so that he might tell everyone how great the power of the God of the Jews is [?]. But soon afterward he met a just slaughter at the hands of his own sons. “Ararat.” This is Armenia.

“And everything in your house will be carried off.” This is because, when he should have shown them God's power and the care he had received from him, he displayed his wealth, which has nothing lasting about it. “All the host of heaven.” The sun, the moon and the stars. “Both ears will ring.” He means that the news will be astonishing to hear.

“The measuring line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab.” I will surround these people too with the same calamities. Famine consumed some of the Samaritans and war others, while others were captured and carried away. And I handed them over to utter destruction, as I did the house of Ahab. “Moreover, Manasseh shed innocent blood.” He made a particular point of killing those who held fast to piety and those who warned him of God's wrath. They say that he also sawed the prophet Isaiah in two. But Chronicles says that he repented and was restored.

“And to the Mazzaroth.” This is the name of a star, probably the Morning Star. “The house of the Kadesim.” He used the same word to call the demons “holy ones,” since Kadesh means “holy.” As has been said, the other translators render “grove” as Asheroth or Ashtaroth, which means Astarte. They set up the image of Aphrodite inside the temple of God. Aquila translated “where the women wove” as “who made garments for those who prostitute themselves.”

“However, the priests of the high places did not go up to the altar of the Lord.” Again he calls “high places” not the altars of idols but the altars of God that stood on the high places. He did not let those of priestly descent go up to the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, but they only ate unleavened bread. If they had served idols, the pious king would not have granted them pardon. “And he defiled Topheth.” In the Hebrew interpretation it means “fall.” It was the place where they made children pass through the fire to Molech, the idol of the Ammonites. “Pharouri” was rendered “of the guard” by those around [?]

“Mosoath [?].” This means “of destruction.” “And the bones of the old prophet were spared.” So he was not a false prophet, or his bones would not have been spared. “There was no king like him.” He said the same about Hezekiah earlier, that no one like him arose after him. If he now ranks Josiah ahead of him, he plainly ranks him ahead of both Hezekiah and David. So here he is not comparing these kings with each other but with the others who were thought to be pious: Asa, Jehoshaphat and Jotham. “Ahaz the son of Josiah.” Jeremiah wrote a more precise [?] account of Ahaz, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah and Zedekiah. He calls Jehoiakim, the son of Jehoiakim, Jeconiah. The book of Chronicles calls him Jehoiakim. The Assyrian released him from prison and had him eat at his table, because God, who had struck him, had healed him.

ON THE FIRST BOOK OF CHRONICLES. PROLOGUE. The writer who took up the present subject put together the things that the writer of Kingdoms left out, as the very name of the book, “Things Left Out,” shows. He collected them from a great many prophetic writings. He also fitted in many things from Kingdoms, because he was eager to keep a single continuous narrative. He traces the genealogy from the beginning, showing that all humanity comes from one man. Since he records only the kingdom of Judah, he teaches which villages and cities belonged to them and where their names came from. From here we learn that Nathan, from whom Luke traces Christ's genealogy, was a full brother of Solomon, the son of David and Bathsheba. He also shows here that Rechab, who is praised in many places in Scripture, was of the tribe of Judah. He says too that Reuben lost the birthright because he defiled his father's bed, and that Joseph received it, while Judah was preferred for leadership because of his surpassing strength, and above all because of the Lord who sprang from him according to the flesh. This is what “for a ruler from him” means. The others were temporary, but this one alone who came forth from him is an eternal king. He also teaches how the tribes beyond the Jordan defeated the foreigners because they hoped in God alone. He gives the genealogy of the priests and Levites as well. He shows that Zadok, who was high priest in David's time, was the eleventh from Aaron, and that Zadok's descendant Azariah was the first to serve as priest after Solomon built the temple. From these came Jehozadak, who was carried off to Babylon after the city was captured. His son was Jeshua, the great priest, who brought the captives back with Zerubbabel. From here we learn that Korah, who rose up against Moses, was his cousin. He was a descendant of Izhar, the son of Kohath and brother of Amram, Moses' father. We also learn that Korah's sons did not share their father's punishment. Indeed, Samuel the great traces his descent from him, and Heman the psalm-singer was a descendant of Samuel, since he was the son of Joel, Samuel's son. Asaph the psalm-singer traced his descent from Gershom, son of Levi and brother of Kohath. And Ethan, one of the singers, traced his descent from Merari, son of Levi. He also explains the difference between priests and Levites. He also gives [?] the cause of the captivity,

since the writer lived after it. In histories you cannot find accounts of things still to come. He also teaches that those foreigners who lived among them had been taken captive in war. The same goes for the priests, the Levites and the Nethinim, who were probably temple servants. Many people, including people from the other tribes, dedicated them to assist the priests and Levites, and they became water-carriers and woodcutters. If the Gibeonites did so, how much more these? Among the Hebrews “Nethinim” is interpreted as “gift of God.” He also says that the inhabitants of Jerusalem came from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh and Levi. He calls the descendants of Korah Korahites. He says that David and Samuel appointed gatekeepers from among them. In this passage he mentioned the tabernacle, since the temple had not yet been built. He also explains the priestly divisions, which served in turns of seven days. Others, he says, were entrusted with the vessels of the service and with all the inanimate things offered at the altar, and the priests prepared the incense. Saul's burial is also described more clearly here, for it says he was laid under the oak of Jabesh, whereas Kingdoms says “under the field of Jabesh.” So is the story of the medium, for it says, “Samuel the prophet answered him.” Clearly God brought about what Saul had sought through sorcery. So Scripture called that apparition, from which Saul sought to learn the future, “Samuel,” whether it was some angel showing his form or the soul of the prophet. God revealed the future through the medium, just as he revealed the plenty and the famine to Pharaoh, and the successive [?] kingdoms of the earth to Nebuchadnezzar. [?] This is what is called a “band” in Kingdoms. “Men who had understanding of their times.” He admired these men for their wisdom and for their foresight, which came not from prophecy but from intelligence.

“And the Lord was angry with Uzzah.” A Levite was not permitted to touch the ark. David was afraid because of this, and he did not bring the ark into the royal house but into the house of Obed-edom. But God showed that he makes no distinction between Israelites and a foreigner and seeks piety alone, and he flooded that house with all kinds of gifts. When David saw this, he brought the ark into the palace, not on a cart but, according to the law, by means of

“And David wore only an ephod.” Yet he was not a priest. Aquila translated the word as “outer garment” and Symmachus as “shoulder-cloak.” But these garments were worn both by priests and by ordinary people. So David, being God-fearing, danced before the ark after laying aside his royal robes, and wore only an ordinary shoulder-cloak, the kind they now call “Arcadian.” For how could he, a God-fearing man, have broken the law?

“Then David first appointed praise to the Lord by the hand of Asaph and his brothers.” That is, with these men leading. He hints that all the psalms are David's. He entrusted the psalms to these men, as “by the hand” shows, and they performed the psalmody continually, lightening the work by taking turns. The tabernacle was at Gibeon, which is why Zadok offered the sacrifices there. How then did David make an altar on Ornan's threshing floor, when the ark was not there? Because of the punishment falling on the people, he hurried to appease God. This is why the history says, “And David could not go before it to seek the Lord, because he hastened away from the sword of the angel of the Lord.” So he dedicated the place of the sacrifice as the site for a temple. The fire from heaven that burned up the sacrifice showed that it was acceptable.

“Because you have shed much blood.” This is meant to turn people away from bloodshed [?]. For God would not have blamed a just killing, since in the case of Phinehas he called such a killing a sacrifice. David says of him, “And Phinehas stood up and made atonement.” Moses and the Levites killed three thousand men after the making of the calf, Samuel killed Agag, and Elijah killed the prophets of Baal. It was fitting, then, that Solomon, the man of peace, who bore the type of Christ, who was going to build the churches throughout the whole world, should build the Jewish temple. For, as Paul says, he is our peace, who has made the two one.

CHAPTER 23. “And the Levites were numbered.” He gives their number and explains how David assigned them to their various duties. He also shows that the descendants of Moses were enrolled among them, and that Zadok the high priest was a descendant of Eleazar, while Ahimelech was a descendant of Ithamar. Because Eleazar's descendants were more numerous, David gave them two shares in the priestly divisions and gave Ithamar's descendants one. Luke also mentions the divisions in the Gospel when he says that Zechariah belonged to the division of Abijah. The present book shows that this Abijah received the seventh lot.

…the leaders of the singers. Some have said that these men were called prophets not of God but of David, because they received the hymns from him and sang them with instruments. But Scripture shows that they too shared in the grace of prophecy, when it says, “Those who prophesied with lyres,” and the rest. And again, “The sons of Asaph, under Asaph the prophet.” And again, it speaks of Jeduthun as one “who prophesied thanksgiving.” And of Heman it says, “the king's seer in the words of God.” He appointed the descendants of Moses as guardians of the sacred treasuries, where the spoils of war and the gifts offered to God were stored. CHAPTER [?]. “To serve as scribes and to judge.” Symmachus has “as instructors and judges.”
“And Benaiah.” This man is a priest. He has the same name as the Benaiah in Kingdoms, the palace commander and the king's nephew, who was evidently of the royal tribe.

CHAPTER 28. “And with a willing soul.” God does not accept forced service, he says. “If you seek him, he will be found by you.” This is the command of the Gospel: “Seek,” it says, “and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” “And the pattern of everything that he had in the spirit.” He teaches that these designs were drawn up not by human reasoning but by the grace of the Spirit. “Kapphoure.” Certain gold and silver vessels in which they mixed the fine flour with oil. “All this in writing from the hand of the Lord.” What he called “in the spirit” above he now calls “from the hand of the Lord.” So the all-holy Spirit is Lord. “Until all the service of the work of the Lord is finished.” He promised him God's care only up to a fixed point. For while Solomon was building he was pious, but once he had finished he turned aside to impiety.

“And who will willingly fill his hands today?” After giving a vast amount of wealth, he urges the leaders to offer gifts to God willingly. And when he sees how eager the people are, he offers God a hymn of thanksgiving. “On the throne of the Lord as king in place of David.” That is, he sat on the throne given by God. He shows how the earlier history ended, and that the prophets Samuel, Nathan and Gad had also written books.

ON THE SECOND BOOK OF CHRONICLES

“And who is able to build him a house?” He shows Hiram his own knowledge of God. For who, he says, will raise a house worthy of God, whom the highest heaven cannot contain? Still, I offer him reverence and honor as far as I am able. Hiram showed how much friendship with the pious benefits a person when he said: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth.” He had evidently already learned from David that the God of Israel is the maker of heaven and earth. The figures given for the measurements of the temple do not disagree with those in Kings, if one adds the twenty cubits of the inner sanctuary to the forty cubits of length, and adds to the twenty-five of height those of the two-storied and three-storied [?]

“From the city of David.” This is what he calls Zion, which David fortified, building the royal palace within its walls. “At the feast.” Clearly the feast of Tabernacles, for, he says, it was the seventh month.

“With the songs of the Lord, which David made.” Again he has taught that the Psalms are David’s. Solomon was pious and would not allow Pharaoh’s daughter to live in the house of David. “For it is holy,” he says, “because the ark of the Lord entered there” [?]. Josephus called the imported timber pine wood, whereas in Kings it is called supports for the house of the Lord and for the king’s house. And the man of God who, he says there, was devoured by the lion, Joel [?]

“And the king did not listen to the people, for the turn of events was from God.” Those whom God cares for, he makes wise about what they must do. Anyone deprived of this is carried along at random. God decided to divide the kingdom because Solomon had sinned. Jeroboam turned [the people?] away from God [?], drove out God’s priests and the Levites [?], and [appointed?] his own [?]

“Sukkiim and Kushiim”: Troglodytes and Ethiopians. “And the rulers were ashamed.” Symmachus has “they admitted they were in the wrong.” For this reason God also turned aside his wrath and did not bring utter destruction on them. “I will grant them,” he says, “a little deliverance.” That is, I will preserve in them the spark of blessing meant for the world. “For my wrath shall not drip upon Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.” That is, I will save the punishment for later. For the present I am laying on them only a yoke of servitude, so that by comparison they may learn how kind my yoke is and how heavy the yoke of men.

“Ought you not to know?” You ought to have known, he says, that the kingdom of David is given by God and has no end, according to God’s promise. How then have you revolted and fallen under a tyrant? He called the firmness of the kingdom an everlasting covenant of salt. For even barbarians keep firmly to agreements when they share the salt of a table. “Like the peoples of the lands [?]”: like the other nations. For they ordain as priests men who are no priests, for gods that are no gods.

CHAPTER 14

“And the high places”: those set up to God on the hills against the law. “And they cut down their villages around Gerar.” Gerar is a city of Palestine, and so a Gerarite saltus is named, near Eleutheropolis, where [?] colonists of the Ethiopians lived, along with certain others called Amazonim [?]. Further on he will name them Libyans, in the words of the prophet Hanani.

“And in that time there will be no peace for anyone who goes out.” He foretells the invasion of the Assyrians. “But he did not remove the high places.” Again, this means those dedicated to God against the law.

“Because he walked in the earlier ways of David his father.” That is, he followed David’s example of virtue at the beginning of his reign. “And his heart was lifted up.” He says this in praise, for he added “in the ways of the Lord.” By one who “offers willingly to the Lord” he means a person who brings offerings not for sins but as gifts

“But good words have been found in you.” He teaches that earlier good deeds lessen the punishments for sins, since the one is weighed against the other. He also teaches that we must avoid all friendship and kinship with the ungodly. The king accepted the rebuke and attended not only to piety but also to good order of every kind. He appointed judges in all the cities and gave them instructions on judging. Over them he set Amariah the priest, through whom they would learn God’s verdict on matters they did not know, and Zebadiah, so that they could refer their decisions to the king, and the Levites to teach the law. For they called those who taught “scribes.” “And the Lord will be with the good.” He did not simply say “with you.”

“And you gave it to the seed of Abraham your friend.” He reminded God of their forefather, so that he might obtain help through the promise made to Abraham. “Will you not judge them?” This is a question. He also confesses his own weakness. “Listen, all Judah, and you who dwell in Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat.” He honored the king by setting him apart from the others and naming him separately. By “those who dwell” he means those from the other

psalm-singers. He places Levites singing hymns, not armed men, at the head of the army. “In Ezion-geber.” It lies by the Indian Sea and is called Berenice. “Because you made friends with Ahaziah.” See how evil kinship ends. For Jehoram, his son, followed the impiety of his father-in-law Ahab and killed all his brothers. And the rest, he says [?]

“In a writing from Elijah.” For Elijah did not come to him in person but made it known by letter. “Because you have not walked in the way of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah.” So these kings were not wholly disapproved. “And those bordering on the Ethiopians.” Further on he calls them Amazonim.
“May the Lord see and judge.” And he was not disappointed in his request, for a year later [Joash] was handed over to the Syrians

“For the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest.” For God said to Noah: “Whoever sheds a man’s blood, his own blood shall be shed in return, because I made man in the image of God.” But they killed him not out of zeal for God but as murderers. That is why Amaziah put them to death.
“Do not let the army of Israel go with you.” Because of their impiety.

“In the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the vision of God.” Clearly there were many men named Zechariah: this one, and the son of Jehoiada, whom Joash stoned. Isaiah seems to speak of the one in Uzziah’s time when he says, as from God: “Get me faithful men as witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Berechiah.” For it is written at the beginning that the vision took place under Uzziah, and Isaiah lived at that time. “The Arabs who dwell on the Rock.” By “the Rock” he means the city called Petra. “His heart was lifted up.” For this reason he seized the priests’ privilege, when he ought to have listened to his forefather David: “Do not destroy to the end.” For this reason he also became leprous and suffered the same fate as Adam, who wanted to be God and lost even his being the image of God. For he sat at home, unable even to act as king.
“Because he had laid bare [?] in Judah.” That is, he taught him what he did not know, teaching him the impiety of the foreign nations.

“And they made atonement for all Israel.” Not only for the two tribes. “By the hand of the prophets.” So David too was a prophet. For after naming David, Gad and Nathan, he added “of the prophets” to cover them all. [?]

“And their brothers the Levites helped them.” Few of the priests had been purified, and they were not enough for the priestly service. So the Levites, who had purified themselves beforehand, took part in the sacred rites. They say this can be seen happening even now. When no presbyter is present and the need is urgent, even a deacon is compelled to give baptism to someone who needs it. Further on he will also tell how, when a great crowd gathered, the Levites were compelled to sacrifice, because the priests were far too few. And because those from Israel had been summoned suddenly, most of those who came had no time to be purified. They ate the Passover and were pardoned because of the king’s piety, even though they had broken the law.

“After these words and this faithfulness, Sennacherib came.” He now teaches that God tests even godly men by allowing them to fall into misfortune, and then resolves their difficulties. He also teaches that those who trust in God must not sit idle but must contribute what they can themselves. So Hezekiah prepared for the war, and after doing everything he could, he said: “With him are arms of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God.” In this way he showed that God cannot be fought against, and that human strength is feeble and short-lived. But after he had won and been exalted, he was brought low, according to the saying, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.” Yet because of his piety he did not see the calamities with his own eyes, for he died before the enemies came. Scripture teaches that it was because of the sun’s going backward that the king of the Babylonians sent to him, to ask him about the wonder that had happened on the earth. “Gihon.” This is what he calls Siloam. “And the Lord left him, to test him.” The passage shows that it is better to boast in the Lord. For when he ought to have told of God’s power, he showed off his transient wealth. The words “to test him, to know what was in his heart” mean: he wanted to lay bare Hezekiah’s thoughts to others. For God alone knows the hearts of men.

“And Manasseh knew that the Lord is God.” This is how discipline benefits those who are willing. “But the people still sacrificed on the high places.” It is clear that he means those who sacrificed to the Lord on high places, for he added: “[?] in vain to their God.”
